speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A decade ago, we restructured the Workforce Development Agency into two agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: WSG remained under MOM to focus on strengthening employment facilitation, services and programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SSG moved under MOE to enable it to work more closely with our institutes of higher learning (IHLs) to drive the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since then, both agencies have come a long way in providing individuals and employers with more comprehensive support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SSG has built a vibrant continuing education and training (CET) landscape, ramping up offerings by private training providers and establishing the IHLs as a key pillar in the ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through the SkillsFuture Credit, SSG has mainstreamed the culture of lifelong learning in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is about one-fifth of the resident workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SSG has also introduced the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, extending significant support for mid-career Singaporeans to pursue a substantive skills reboot.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: WSG has expanded its reach in supporting individuals and employers through employment facilitation, reskilling and job redesign.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: WSG helped many Singaporeans to overcome episodes of economic slowdown, such as the recent COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: WSG has also expanded the range of support, with the introduction of the Polaris programme to support individuals in long-term career planning in an increasingly fast-changing labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The 2016 restructuring substantially delivered what it set out to do.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But over the last 10 years, the world around us has shifted, and the next 10 years will certainly not in any way resemble the last 10.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, technology is advancing at an unprecedented pace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) that we see today would have been science fiction in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But the technological wave is now here, it is upon us and it is picking up speed and momentum.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, geopolitical shocks are reshaping the global economy in ways that were difficult to imagine a decade ago.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since 2016, we have lived through a global pandemic that shuttered economies overnight.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Wars in Europe and now in the Middle East have upended energy markets and a rupture in US-China relations is redrawing the map of global trade and investment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The more predictable world that our 2016 framework rested on is now gone.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By 2030, it will be one in four.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While we had seen this demographic change coming, we are now feeling its impact more acutely.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This further sharpens the imperative for us to strengthen the career longevity of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In short, we live in a different world from 10 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What worked in the past decade will need significant transformation, to be more predictive, to be more anticipatory, as well as be more responsive and targeted moving forward.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will call the new agency the "Skills and Workforce Development Agency" (SWDA).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The name reflects the agency's mission to develop and to advance Singapore's human potential.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will focus on better serving individuals and employers and better partnering the broader ecosystem of providers of career and employment services as well as training.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the world we live in today, many of us are worried about whether our job will still exist in time to come; whether we can find another job with the same pay and seniority if we lose our jobs; whether our skills built up over an entire career may become obsolete faster than we can keep up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But our collective response, how do we respond to it, must be one of proactive action, not passive anxiety.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will enable Singaporeans to take purposeful action to stay adaptable, to stay resilient in a fast-changing and uncertain economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will support you to build up your career health consistently, strengthening immunity to disruptions and instilling agility to seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will help you to make better training and career decisions in support of your longer-term career goals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will help you to bounce back after facing career setbacks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And SWDA will do all of these by bringing the capabilities of SSG and WSG together, integrating them to deliver timely and trusted career and skills insights with smarter training and career services, and do that even more than before.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will build a more comprehensive offering of tools, services and programmes to journey with individuals through different life stages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For fresh graduates navigating your first steps in the job market, SWDA will expand opportunities for you to gain real work experience and secure your footing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will partner companies to provide attachment and traineeship programmes that will give you concrete work experience and exposure, which will then create pathways for you to enter growth sectors with strong manpower demand.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will develop new or expand existing programmes, like the BioPharma Talent Builder programme, which equips you to take on jobs in leading biomedical firms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For those still uncertain about your career trajectory after graduation, SWDA will offer career guidance to help you identify potential career pathways in line with your aspirations, your goals and your values.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For mid-career workers, whether facing mid-career stagnations, feeling apprehensive about being displaced, encountering retrenchments, or returning to work after a caregiving break or simply planning ahead, the hardest part is often not knowing where to start and when to take the first step.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will enhance career guidance, will enhance job matching and reskilling support to provide more transition pathways.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This includes expanding partnerships with private career service providers and employer networks to deliver more resources for you to navigate the labour market, help you make personalised career plans and connect to new prospects.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will continue to expand and improve on these service offerings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For senior workers who have much to contribute with your networks and your experience, and if you are keen to do so, SWDA is part of the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment that is developing an integrated approach to support longer careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Working with progressive companies and human resource professionals, SWDA will develop and will scale solutions for longer, multi-stage careers and promote age-inclusive jobs and workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, preparing our workforce for AI is a key priority.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is one of the priorities that SWDA will deliver in the coming months, as part of a holistic suite of efforts to help workers future-proof their skills and strengthen career health in an AI-enabled economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will offer individuals a more seamless journey through an integrated touchpoint.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead of navigating programmes offered by two agencies, individuals will now have a single interface to the full suite of career guidance, skills training and job matching support offered by SWDA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will offer an enhanced digital experience, with AI-powered personalised career guidance, recommendations of in-demand training courses, and exploratory tools for employment opportunities based on one's portfolio of skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, the other part of our equation, which is a big one – and that is for employers, SWDA can provide support for their recruitment efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For those employers' business looking to fill job vacancies, SWDA can help to accelerate hiring of suitable candidates from its pool of jobseekers and trainees, leveraging the Careers and Skills Passport as a common verified information source on the work experience and the skillsets of candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will also be a stronger partner to employers in workforce development.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By unifying skills intelligence with labour market data, it will give businesses sharper, more actionable insights and modalities to support skills-first workforce planning, hiring and internal mobility.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will support the delivery of training that is more relevant to the needs of employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA's suite of programmes can help employers reskill employees to transfer to new job roles, hence, expanding the pool of available candidates beyond external hires.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond recruitment and training, SWDA will support employers through the challenges of deeper workforce transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As AI continues to reshape job roles and business models, SWDA will provide employers with integrated support across workforce restructuring, job redesign and capability development.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Overall, the aim is to help businesses plan more effectively, hire more confidently and adapt their workforce more quickly to evolving needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the Financial Services sector, WSG, the Monetary Authority of Singapore and Institute of Banking and Finance launched a Jobs Transformation Map (JTM) on Generative AI for Financial Services, partnering 11 financial institutions to unpack what AI adoption means for specific job roles and showcase the opportunities for employees that job redesign and reskilling can potentially bring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The JTM showed how finance and insurance companies can reshape roles in customer service, relationship management and risk management, improving productivity and enabling employees to move up the value chain.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It also highlighted new job opportunities in areas such as AI governance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will bring this approach to support transformation in other sectors, including adoption of AI and managing its impact on jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In sum, whether you are dealing with urgent manpower issues for the here and now, or growing your team to expand operations, or even restructuring your workforce to support a pivot in your business, SWDA will work with you, will partner you to transform your business and your workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, SWDA will strengthen the ecosystem of service providers of career and employment services and training.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SSG has already built up a strong training sector over the past decade.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will bolster other parts of this ecosystem that serve workers and employers on their career as well as their workforce needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This includes recruitment agencies, staffing agencies, career coaching and career guidance providers, human resources (HR) consultancy, technology firms, online job portals and the like.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will work with industry to raise the quality standards, improve accessibility and develop new solutions by spurring both innovation and collaboration.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our goal ultimately is a vibrant private sector, complemented with public employment services and programmes that will be a catalyst and enabler for broad-based workforce transformation and adaptation, amidst the rapid changes in our labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Last year, we launched the Alliance for Action on Advancing Career and Employment Services (AfA-ACES) comprising representatives from this ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are also pilots to work with employers to design more flexible work models and adopt skills-based practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These pilots may give rise to new programmes and services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: More importantly, through these pilots, we are discovering together the strengths of our ecosystem today and the opportunities to take it to the next level tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Later this year, the AfA-ACES will release its recommendations, which will chart plans to transform the ecosystem to serve individuals and employers more effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is something that I will appeal to everyone because it requires a whole-of-society approach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In an era where AI is rapidly transforming job requirements at a pace that no single institution can fully anticipate, lifelong learning and career health must become the norm and it must become a practical reality.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It must be something that Singaporeans can and should invest in and take ownership of throughout their entire working life and is not a resource that you can turn to only when the circumstances compel you to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers too should continuously invest in your employees' career health so that your employees are well-equipped to contribute to the success of your business.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The aspiration is to build a Singapore workforce that meets change with confidence, one that is oriented not merely towards managing disruption, but towards seizing the opportunities that come with it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, not one that is responsive and reactive but one that is preemptive and proactive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SWDA will work with our tripartite partners to catalyse this shift, building on the SkillsFuture movement and the Career Health SG initiative under it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This entails talking about lifelong learning and career health regularly, including at the workplace, internalising it and promoting good career health habits.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This requires training and career guidance to be very accessible to the broad middle.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our assurance to every worker and every employer is this: work with us, and we will walk with you.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government and our tripartite partners will be with you, every step of the way.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Part 1 of the Bill introduces the terms used in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Part 2 establishes SWDA as a Statutory Board and describes the functions and powers of SWDA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Parts 3 to 6 set out SWDA's governance structures and requirements, which are aligned with the Public Sector (Governance) Act 2018.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They cover the membership, the appointment and decision-making procedures of the SWDA Board, as well as personnel and financial matters.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Parts 7 and 8 set out the enforcement powers necessary for the administration of the Bill and its general provisions, including the power to make regulations and to issue codes of practice or guidelines for providers of career and employment services and training.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Part 9 provides for the transfer of undertakings and employees from WSG and SSG to SWDA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have been closely engaging and supporting all officers, to ensure that both their well-being and career aspirations are well-cared for amidst this transition.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The refreshed mission of SWDA will provide new growth opportunities and career pathways for staff.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also provide opportunities for officers to equip themselves for new job roles, so that no one will inadvertently fall through the cracks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The key amendments are to the Private Education Act and Skills Development Levy Act, which will be administered by SWDA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At its heart, the Bill affirms a conviction that this House has long held – that every Singaporean, at every stage of his or her working life, deserves support to grow, to adapt and to contribute to the nation's continued success.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With this, Mr Deputy Speaker, I seek to move.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: She is in her 50s and has worked as an HR administrator for over 20 years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: She told me, "Ms Yeo, I am not worried about robots taking my job, I just want to know that there is something thinking about what comes next for me." That quiet anxiety is something we all hear often on the ground: not panic, not resistance, just a very human need to know that someone is watching out for you.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I support it and want to speak to what it must achieve, not as policy, but as lived experience.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I declare my role as the Executive Secretary of the National Transport Workers Union, the Assistant Secretary-General of the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and Chairman of the Manpower Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And these are the lenses that I am using to speak on.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Today, careers are longer but no longer linear.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The idea of one employer, one skillset, one trajectory belongs to an earlier generation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: What took years to build can be reshaped within a few.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: So, the challenge is no longer just training workers or helping them find jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is ensuring that training leads to jobs, jobs lead to wage growth and transformation produces gains that are shared with workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is the gap this Bill is designed to close.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As Manpower GPC Chairman, I recently visited three companies with my fellow GPC members to understand how tech-enabled, AI-powered business transformation and workforce upskilling are actually playing out on the ground, in real workplaces, with real workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I want to share what I saw, because these visits were not just informative.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Each company showed a different face of Singapore's workforce and, together, they speak to why SWDA's mandate is as important as it is.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: At SMRT, I witnessed what happens when a large employer commits fully to workforce transformation as a cultural and operational mission.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: SMRT has institutionalised the kaizen philosophy – a Japanese yet universal concept of continuous, incremental improvement – as a unifying mindset across all levels of the organisation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Layered onto this, SMRT has adopted technology to unlock operational efficiencies – managing worker fatigue, boosting safety through predictive maintenance and redesigning workflows to reduce the physical burden on staff.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Workers who have spent decades on the job, who know every quirk of the system, every subtle sound that signals a problem and now working smarter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is the promise of how continuous learning ensures that technology is done right: not replacing experienced workers but augmenting them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Giving them tools that honour their expertise, extending their working lives and rewarding their commitment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I call on SWDA to support more companies, like SMRT, to ensure that workplace cultures support lifelong learning and to reward workers when they walk the talk.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And Mr Deputy Speaker, as a Member of Parliament for Punggol group representation constituency (GRC), I felt a particular sense of pride that this innovation is rooted right here in our Punggol community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: What I want to highlight is not the AI, impressive as it is, but how the transformation was designed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Staff was not presented with a finished product and told to adapt.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They were involved from the beginning – shaping service design, store navigation, check-out and backend operations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Many of these frontline staff are women, including mid-career returnees who came back to work after years of caregiving, not the typical profile technology is designed for.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Yet because FairPrice chose to design with them rather than for them, the result is a system that works for staff and customers alike.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When workers are treated as co-creators rather than recipients of change, transformation is smoother, adoption is faster and outcomes are better.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: SWDA must champion co-design not as a nice-to-have, but as a defining feature of how Singapore approaches workforce transformation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We know AI will reshape our workforce and our workplaces, but how it unfolds in practice will depend on pioneers on the ground.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: My Manpower GPC colleagues and I saw this firsthand at FairPrice – a company willing to reimagine not just its own operations, but the broader retail cluster.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They have taken bold steps to reimagine not just their own operations, but the broader retail cluster, helping workers and Singaporeans begin to see and experience what an AI-enabled workplace could look like.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: So, my call to SWDA is this: support more of such companies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Enable them to experiment, to learn and to lead to boldly go where no one has gone before.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And in doing so, light the way for their sectors and for Singapore's future of work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Chye Thiam Maintenance is a homegrown company many of us would recognise from the orange and yellow vehicles that keep our estates, malls and highways clean.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: From a small family outfit, they have grown into a team of 3,500 strong.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Over the decades, they have continued investing in technology and machinery and at every stage, their workers moved forward with these changes, not out of them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In the past two years, they introduced robo-sweepers and autonomous service vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But the real story is what came with it – job redesign, skills upgrading and new roles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is a small but important signal, that when work changes, we recognise and reward it differently.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It raised the quality of jobs, creating pathways for seniors and lower-wage workers to move into safer, more skilled and better-paying jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For Chye Thiam Maintenance, embracing technology also brought in more business and with it, the ability to hire more and uplift more.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is the virtuous cycle we want to see: when innovation drives both enterprise growth and worker progression.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Chye Thiam Maintenance is also an accredited training organisation, working with our agencies to build structured training programmes tailored to their workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: What they have done is to build a wage and career ladder with support and guidance from our agencies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As a local company, Chye Thiam Maintenance shows us that with the right intent and support from the Government, transformation can be inclusive – not by asking workers to simply "keep up", but by enabling them to move forward.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Across all three companies, a common theme emerges.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These employers adopted AI and technology to transform their businesses without leaving their workers behind.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They built a culture of employee stake-holding in transformation and one of lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Supported by grants and partnerships, they took on the responsibility of designing and delivering training.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And their workers came out on the other side with better conditions, new skills and wage growth.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is the model exactly that Singapore needs to scale.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I am confident that our ecosystem partners stand ready to work alongside SWDA in this – the Tripartite Jobs Council, our trade associations and chambers, employment agencies, and our unions, of course.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They are already embedded in companies and communities across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They have the trust of workers and employers built up over years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: SWDA must build on this, not bypass it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I want to make this call specifically: SWDA must establish regular, ongoing engagement with these stakeholders not just at the point of policy design, but continuously.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The world of work is changing faster than any policy cycle.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Policies that are not continuously grounded become policies that do not work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: SWDA is also well-positioned to drive research to develop a data-driven view of jobs of the future and to deliver design grants that supercharge company transformation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This research role is important and I welcome it, particularly as companies and sectors embark on their starship enterprise reimagination journeys with their workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Indeed, to go boldly where no one else has gone before.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But in implementing transformation, SWDA must be a champion of a human-centric, worker-centric approach.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This will make the difference between transformation that works for people, and transformation that works for productivity metrics alone.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These are composite sketches drawn from real ground conversations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Joanne, not her real name, spent nearly a decade out of the workforce, first caring for her young children, then for her mother who had a stroke.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When she finally could return to work, she came to see me.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: She had real skills, genuine experience and she was ready.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But her retirement savings were depleted from years without Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: She had a caregiving gap in her resume and she needed to undergo re-training but had no financial buffer to sustain her through it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our NTUC's C U Back @ Work programme has shown us that this model works.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: SWDA must build on this, not reinvent it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And it must make these pathways permanent and accessible to all the Joannes across the whole entire island, not just those few lucky ones who were lucky enough to find their way to us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Sakthi – not his real name, but he will recognise himself – is a bus captain.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: He has been on the road for over 20 years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: He takes pride in his work and his passengers know him by name.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But here is what most commuters do not know.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Between runs, some breaks are as short as six minutes and he starts his day at 4.30 am.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: He can drive up to 16 runs in a day.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And at 60 years old, the fatigue is real and it can be a safety matter, not just only a welfare one.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Older workers are experienced contributors who deserve workplaces designed with them in mind and not around them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: David, not his real name, was a mid-career IT professional when his company restructured.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: He knows the window is open, but he cannot afford to stop driving.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: His family needs the income now, not after he has completed the training programme.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Joanne, Sakthi and David, they are not unusual cases.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And 10 years from now, I hope we will look back on this Bill as the moment Singapore chose to ensure that our next bound of growth is one that every worker can be part of.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: To my resident at the Meet-the-People Session who just wants to know that someone is thinking about what comes next for her, I want to say: This is exactly what we are here to do today.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I declare my interest as the owner and director of a company that provides software to training providers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, it has the potential to eliminate institutional silos.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This lowers the risk of skills development and training occurring without an active alignment to available job frequencies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, it could prevent fragmented journeys of jobseekers, reducing the friction for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Who previously had to navigate disparate digital platforms and physical agency locations for career coaching and skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, it could resolve data administrative silos by integrating the training records formerly held by Skills Future Singapore, with employment and placement records held by WSG.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This integration has the potential to empower career coaches to provide holistic data-driven interventions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister just explained that WSG may remain under MOM to focus on strengthening employment facilitation services and programmes, while SSG moved under MOE to enable it to work more closely with our IHLs to drive the skills future movement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is not clear to me why WDA had to split in order to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The new agency's functions straddle both education and manpower.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, no current political office holder spans both Ministries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does the Prime Minister intend to appoint a bridging political office holder, such as a Minister of State for Manpower and Education?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bill's Explanatory Note states that the Bill will not involve the Government in any extra financial expenditure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But surely, the cost of this re-merger will not be zero.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bill specifies that the agency will provide for or facilitate the provision of career advisory and employment assistance services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Would the SWDA be providing job search assistance directly under this new integrated agency model?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the Government relies heavily on third parties, such as the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) and other private career matching providers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the SWDA were to directly provide these services, it would be able to leverage its access to MOM data regarding labour market mismatches and real time hiring trends to adapt assistance in a more timely fashion to rapid economic shifts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How would the Government ensure performance accountability of the job search assistance provided by these external partners?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Job search assistance should not merely involve resume touch-ups and pointing job seekers to employment portals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government commit to a more intensive assistance in the job search process, particularly for those who have experienced persistent structural unemployment despite their most earnest efforts?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Today, many jobseekers apply for dozens of jobs daily without customising their resumes to the specific job descriptions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In parallel, organisations utilise automated tracking systems that filter applications strictly by their degree of match with the job description, sometimes discarding all applications did that that do not meet at least a 90% keyword match.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Consequently, many qualified applicants may not get a call-up for the interview.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will SWDA require job assistance programmes to guide job seekers on such technical skills?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will SWDA officers take on a more active role in bridging the gap between employer needs and candidate profiles?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For instance, if the agency identifies a candidate whose profile closely matches a job description, will officers proactively pitch this candidate to the employer and advocate for them to be considered for an interview?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the onus ultimately remains on the candidate to prove their worth during the interview, this active matching by the agency would at least help jobseekers get their foot in the door.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Job assistance programmes should also actively bridge skills gaps in networking and help jobseekers leverage professional connections.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such skills are critically important and often not taught in formal schooling.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bill in clause 68 specifies the transfer of properties, rights and liabilities, which inherently includes the vast network of educational initiatives and career guidance programmes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Students should be exposed to different careers earlier, ideally starting at lower secondary level when they will be choosing their GCE "O" and "N" level subjects.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This early intervention will steer students away from simply settling for subjects or courses they have no genuine interest in because they do not know any better.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Would the SWDA work directly with schools to provide systematic and regular career guidance or exposure to students?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would shift the burden of career guidance away from teachers and allow students to have some exposure to industry experts as they decide on what career best works for their individual goals and talents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would not only lead to better personal outcomes but also yield better long-term workforce outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must shift the admissions waiting towards an applicant's demonstrated passion and aptitude for a specific field, rather than relying too heavily on relative academic grade cut-offs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, will the Government work with the IHLs to afford students greater flexibility to make mid-stream switches in their educational journeys without the fear of having to start from scratch?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will go some way in creating a workforce of the future that is adaptable, brave and agile.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, these measures will minimise the systemic waste of public and private resources that occurs when graduates abandon courses and careers they were never genuinely interested in pursuing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, I turn to the harmonisation with other partners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the Bill successfully merges functions that currently sit in MOM and MOE, the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) remains an underlying driver that sets the industry transformation maps (ITMs).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The agency has been described as a job skills integrator.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the roadmap for our industries is set by the ITMs under MTI.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the Minister be able to address the potential risks that by merging MOM and MOE functions, we are simply creating a new larger silo that is disconnected from MTI's strategic planning?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Would the agency be tracking the performance of this initiative and help train the job ambassadors?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would therefore suggest the Ministry consider the following KPIs for the agency as a starting framework to ensure better accountability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Public expenditure must be rigorously tracked against its economic purpose.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must move beyond simply tracking whether a jobseeker found any employment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The agency should expand the existing training quality and outcomes measurement surveys to measure whether workers are actively applying the newly acquired competencies in their roles six months after they complete the course.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By doing so, we ensure that every public dollar spent genuinely contributes to a successful job placement or career advancement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: SWDA should be required to publish these outcome-based figures annually.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, the percentage of subsidised training enrolments in courses mapped to documented Shortage Occupation List occupations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Parliament should be able to see year-on-year whether the public's training dollars are flowing towards gaps our economy has already documented.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government now publishes aggregate figures for these.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These aggregated figures will better hold the agency and its service providers to account.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are the logical extension of data that SWDA will already hold.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The integration the Bill promises makes these metrics achievable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The question is whether the Government is prepared to track and publish them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Administrative neatness means little to the displaced mid-career worker stuck in a job search black hole or the young student pressured into an educational path they have no passion for.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The true test of the SWDA will not be how smoothly it integrates its backend systems, but its courage to embrace transparent KPIs, its willingness to proactively champion our job seekers and its agility to move at the speed of our economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If we are reversing a decade's old policy in the name of deeper synergy, the Government must ensure that this synergy actually translates into tangible, measurable resilience for Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.45 pm until 4.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Integrating WSG and SSG strengthens the effectiveness of Singapore's workforce and skills development ecosystem, and attests to the Government's ability and agility in responding to change in our labour landscape.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Last year marked 10 years since the national SkillsFuture movement was launched to promote lifelong learning as a national priority.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this House, I called for a timely review of services delivered across WSG, SSG and other arms like the IHLs and NTUC's e2i, to reduce duplication of resources and provide even more seamless end-to-end support for workers, jobseekers and employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am glad that this call has been heard.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The creation of SWDA responds to trends like increased geopolitical and economic volatility, new technologies and diverse career aspirations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Rationalising the ambits of WSG and SSG provides a strategic window to critically assess what has worked and what has not.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Identifying where the gaps are, who are the underserved and what are the bold steps we need to take to ensure our workers stay afloat, abreast and ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To this end, I offer three priorities for the next bound of Singapore's skills and workforce development ecosystem, what I call the three "highs", not "Hi" but "high" – high speed, high quality and high returns.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This refers to speed-to-market for training curriculum when new skills become in-demand and career transition programmes when industries face sunset.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In a fast-changing and highly competitive global labour landscape, the earliest bird catches the best worm.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SWDA will need to accelerate operational speed by reducing administrative burden, sharing data analytics and consolidating support packages into a "one-stop shop" experience for anyone, anytime and anywhere.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The success of this vision will depend on faster rather than slower clearance chains with joint oversight.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SWDA must also make clear to employers that delays in early job redesign and training investment will compound real costs through widening skills gap, tardy transformation and weakened competition positions, while early adopters who step up will reap strong gains and benefits.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This can be made possible by closer integration of training design with company training and transformation committees to ensure a smoother training-to-work journey for in-service workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Furthermore, proactively undertaking job redesign can also ensure more immediate fit for freshly trained new hires, especially mid-career trainees whose freshly acquired skills, and track-record experience in critical thinking and business problem solving present good value to prospective employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: High speed also in absorbing shocks, is also key during times of geopolitical and economic volatility, which are set to persist.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government has done this well, for example, through the Singapore Economic Resilience Taskforce and Homefront Crisis Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, I urge that more can be done to support impacted workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Business restructuring and AI-driven disruption have slowed hiring and growth of entry-level jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Graduates across our autonomous universities (AUs), including our private education institutions in the past year, secured fewer full-time positions across the board.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For example, job matching and career guidance services can be integrated with the JS scheme to fulfil the vision of being a "one-stop shop" for involuntarily unemployed workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, we must also be mindful that what is considered useful is different to every learner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Apart from audit compliance and learner satisfaction, high-quality job-related learning must mean industry application or validation, such as employer co-design, work-integrated learning, like attachments or paid-per-task opportunities, portfolio building and access to mentorship or networking.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These increase potential employment outcomes for learners while allowing employers to assess candidates with lower risk.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This includes safeguards to ensure fair allowances, reasonable work hours and safe and meaningful tasks.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Investing in high quality student internships will benefit the same employers when graduates enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On paper, this should translate into a highly productive and skilled workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is worthwhile asking: do the returns justify our investments?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Granted, returns may be hard to quantify, as they go beyond employment outcomes, wage progression and training participation rates among vulnerable worker segments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Investing in a culture of lifelong learning and employment support has ripple effects on the resilience and diversity of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In Singapore, we do not have a shortage of funding or initiatives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our workforce and skills development ecosystem has matured beyond the experimental, piloting phase.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can SWDA also share its plans to successfully integrate jobs and skills infrastructure and management strategy to increase return on investment?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Time, skills and qualifications mismatches were raised as a point of concern in NTUC's recently released two-year study with the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) on underemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SWDA can develop a robust and centralised tracking system to track longitudinal outcomes of its various courses, programmes and credit schemes as well as workers' career health to ensure returns commensurate with cost.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To conclude, the creation of SWDA holds powerful potential for a higher speed, higher quality and higher returns skills and workforce development ecosystem, given the successful integration of jobs and skills infrastructure and management strategy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I encourage SWDA to boldly reimagine what learning and working can look like for the next generation and plant seeds early, just as the Government did with WSG and SSG over a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I also invite SWDA to leverage the Tripartite Jobs Council as it operates within the wider workforce ecosystem to transform skills and jobs, because this will be SWDA's key ground like into the heart of workplaces and worker groups.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can Singapore become a leader in innovative and inclusive learning practices, such as peer learning through communities of practice, residency programmes and incubators for non-traditional career aspirations or non-traditional learners, like caregivers, seniors and persons with disabilities?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can Singapore accomplish a triple-win by fostering a workforce with higher productivity, higher resilience and higher flexibility to meet the needs of workers, learners and employers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If we continue to be proactive rather than reactive, I believe we can.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must remember that today, we no longer just learn, work and retire.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We learn, work, learn, work, learn, work, and maybe, retire.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin): Mr Speaker, I support the establishment of the Skills and Workforce Development Authority.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that this newly established statutory board will operate in bold and innovative ways across three areas to meet the changing needs of the world and the Artificial Intelligence transition, so no Singaporean is left behind.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, we need to make job redesign a priority.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This reflects a concern: that employers will integrate AI into existing workflows rather than begin with employees' well-being in mind by making their future work more valuable, meaningful and sustainable.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I therefore hope that the SWDA will invest more resources in and place greater emphasis on job redesign by making it a priority that will strengthen the competitiveness of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, I hope the SWDA can address the gaps in Singapore's skills-based hiring model.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many surveys have found that the majority of Singapore employers still focus on the applicants' academic qualifications and certificates rather than their skills.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As one of the largest employers, the Government has also yet to begin tracking data on how many Public Service job advertisements include or omit academic qualification requirements.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that as the Government leads the private sector in promoting skills-based hiring, it will also publish relevant data in tandem – for example, by tracking how many employers have adopted a skills-first approach in their recruitment process.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, and more importantly, when publishing data to measure the achievements of the new agency, we should do so from the perspective of Singaporeans and examine the tangible impact on their lives.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For employees, we should be measuring whether taking courses using the SkillsFuture training grant has improved employment outcomes – for instance, whether their salaries have increased – rather than simply tracking how many people have enrolled in programmes or utilised subsidies.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For employers', we should track whether productivity has improved after job redesign, rather than looking at whether employees have attended training courses or whether companies have received subsidies.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The establishment of this new agency is a fresh starting point.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope we can also seize this opportunity to write a new chapter for the future of Singapore's employment and workforce – one that is told from the perspective of workers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, much of the conversation about workforce development and transformation has come from individuals who are senior enough to shape their organisations or by economists and academics looking at workforce transformation or the workforce from the macro perspective.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I would like to offer a view from the middle.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I speak as a millennial worker who has spent almost nine years in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have spent my working life, so far, as an individual contributor, someone who implements strategic decisions more than I make them – a team member who is good at her job, but rarely at the table where such decisions are made.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From where I stand, a lot of what workers have heard about workforce transformation has been directed at us.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are told, embrace new technology – learn, use, master.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Workers are the ones whose livelihoods are on the line.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we are only one side of the transformation equation.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, today, I want to talk about how the new SWDA must also hold employers accountable.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, job redesign is buried in a sub-clause under section 5 of the Bill, which outlines the new agency's functions.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is defined as the review and re-allocation by an employer of duties and tasks among employees.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I looked up where this definition could have come from.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears to have been taken word for word from the 2003 Workforce Singapore Agency Act.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the 23-year-old definition still adequate for the age of AI?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Job redesign, today, cannot simply mean re-allocating tasks between employees.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given what technology can do now, what should people be doing instead?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the difference between a company that adopts AI by simply layering it onto existing workflows and hoping for the best, versus one that considers which parts of a job can be transformed, automated or augmented by technology, and then deliberately shaping the human role into something more valuable, purposeful and sustainable.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Workers have put in time, effort and money into acquiring new skills, but too often they return to a job market only to be filtered out because they do not have the right paper qualifications or past job titles.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The evidence tells us that we have a challenge with employer behaviour.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is in employer adoption of skills-first hiring practices.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The index findings confirmed what a 2023 Boston Consulting Group's Skills-Based Hiring Trend Report had already shown.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the United States (US), UK and Australia had all reduced degree requirements when hiring for university-level jobs between 2017 and 2022, Singapore moved in the opposite direction.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While much has been said about making skills-based hiring a priority – and I recognise the groundwork done by introducing the skills-based hiring handbook and establishing the Centre for Skills-First Practices – it is unclear whether any of this has materially changed how Singapore employers hire.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I filed a Parliamentary Question last November, asking what percentage of Public Service jobs waived formal academic qualifications and employers' skills-based assessment as a primary hiring criterion.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the new agency work with the Public Service to lead the adoption of skills-based hiring across public sector jobs?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having already released relevant toolkit to support employers, will the new agency now commit to tracking and posting statistics on the adoption of skills-based hiring by Singapore employers?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could begin with a baseline that tracks the proportion of skills-based job postings, broken down by sector and employers' size.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans should be able to see year-on-year whether hiring culture is genuinely shifting or whether we still are, as the OECD Index found, bound by a stubborn paper ceiling.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My third and final ask, Mr Speaker, is perhaps the most important – measure what genuinely changes in workers' lives and not just what the agency has done.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, we have gotten very good accounting output: how many individuals assisted?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These numbers appear in annual reports, announced with pride.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But does the completed course means that a worker's prospects have actually improved?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the formation of a Company Training Committee mean a company has genuinely transformed?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I want to propose a simple but demanding shift from measuring output to tracking outcomes.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the individual worker level, we should track wage progression and job retention.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Track what proportion of SkillsFuture Credits were used for training that resulted in demonstrable career benefits, not just the uptake of SkillsFture programmes but the programmes' impact on workers' lives.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the employer level, track whether companies are actually redesigning jobs and seeing productivity gains, not just sending staff for courses to access grants.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Track if companies are hiring differently, valuing demonstrated skills.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are they also less likely to conduct retrenchments because they invested in their people before a downturn?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They require follow-through and some courage in data collection.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The agency should also publish anonymised employer level outcome data by sector and by company size.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let Singaporeans see who is genuinely transforming and who is performing transformation.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the workforce level, track whether anxiety is coming down and resilience is going up.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Track whether wages and productivity are moving in tandem.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the benefits of transformation reaching workers across the income and skills spectrum, or whether they are concentrating as they often do at the top?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the new agency's annual report will from day one commit to tracking these outcomes rather than cataloguing programmes launched.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we cannot measure it, we cannot improve it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And Mr Speaker, I want to now close where I started – as a Singaporean worker watching this transformation unfold from the middle.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we need now is not more inspiration or encouragement.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need a system that holds employers and that moves employers and workers forward together, and that holds both sides to account, one where upskilling leads somewhere, where hiring is fair and where success is measured, not in programmes run but in lives that have durably improved.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new SWDA carries a mandate that workers have heard different versions of before and that is precisely why it should do things differently.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For many of my residents – mid-career PMETs navigating transitions, older workers trying to stay relevant, caregivers balancing work and family, younger workers facing contract roles and SMEs struggling with manpower constraints – this Bill can have real, practical implications.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It reshapes how Singapore supports workers and employers at a time when economic change is accelerating amidst disruptions driven by AI and technical advancements as well as geopolitical uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Merging two agencies is a major organisational change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will service levels be set and monitored during this period to ensure that workers and employers are not adversely impacted?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Residents often share the challenges they face navigating multiple touchpoints for training, job matching and career guidance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This Bill strengthens career guidance, training and job matching by giving the new agency explicit statutory functions from providing career advisory services, to developing and accrediting training, to delivering employment facilitation – enabling a fully integrated end-to-end support system for every individual.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With integration, I am glad to hear the Minister assuring that the agency will strengthen personalised career coaching for mid-career and older workers as they face the steepest barriers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clause 5 gives the new agency clear statutory powers to support workers facing sectoral disruptions through career transitions, targeted training pathways and job-matching.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Workers in certain sectors like aviation, retail, hospitality, logistics and administrative roles have faced rapid changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The new agency can be proactive rather than reactive to better anticipate sectoral shifts as well as work with employers and design training aligned with real hiring needs, for sectors undergoing sectoral transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many workers, especially caregivers, need modular, flexible or part time options.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How will the new agency ensure that these flexible options meet industry-recognised outcomes, deliver clear learning outcomes and remain aligned with employer and sector needs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is important because it ensures that workers who need flexibility are not disadvantaged, and that the skills they acquire remain credible and valued in the labour market.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have previously shared feedback from our young residents which indicate an increasing trend of younger workers entering the workforce through contract roles, or have employment disrupted due to business restructuring or transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many have shared with me the anxieties and the challenges they face re-entering the workforce after their contracts end, or when their roles evolve or are phased out.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A lot has been said about AI and the Minister too shared on this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: AI is reshaping job roles across every sector, and workers need timely, coordinated support to navigate these changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clause 5 of the Bill equips the new agency to identify emerging needs early and develop and accredit training and provide career guidance for workers whose roles are being transformed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can I ask the Minister to also share what the agency can do to help workers understand how AI will affect their roles, access relevant training early and transition into new or redesigned jobs with confidence?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will the agency proactively monitor emerging AI trends and their impact on job roles and skills requirements?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And how will the agency work with employers, unions, sector agencies and technology partners to identify early signals of job transformation, update the skills frameworks ahead of time and most importantly, ensure workers receive timely guidance and training before disruptions take hold?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: SMEs often tell us that they are overwhelmed by multiple schemes and processes and a single integrated agency will simplify this experience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A clear and streamlined interface for employers is essential if we want job redesign, training grants and manpower advisory to be easily accessible, especially for SMEs who often lack dedicated HR capacity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill provides the foundation which empower the new agency to offer integrated manpower advisory, workforce upgrading support and enables coordination across job redesign, training and grant programmes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This creates the basis for a single, coherent touchpoint for employers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Minister did share that there would alignment of skills development with labour market data and integrated workforce development and transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A challenge that employers frequently face is that training does not always match real operational needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is this ecosystem alignment – not structure alone – that will determine whether the agency can deliver on the full promise of the Bill and provide meaningful, timely support for both workers and employers as our economy continues to transform.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A key point I pick up throughout the Minister's speech is that while the integration of SSG and WSG is important, it is the role it plays in building and strengthening the ecosystem that is critical.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And Mr Speaker, I stress this point because I think it is a recognition that one agency cannot the panacea to solve all problems and the recognition that it takes all of us.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think the Minister touched on this about the need for a mindset and a cultural change and a partnership.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It will be really a whole shift in how all parties work together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we get it right, we can build a more responsive, integrated and future ready ecosystem that helps workers navigate disruption with confidence and enables employers, especially our SMEs, to transform and grow.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SSG has built a culture of lifelong learning and expanded access to training.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: WSG has evolved from a placement agency into one that supports career guidance, transitions and employability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Taken together, they have supported many workers and firms, and have laid the foundation for a more resilient workforce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, AI and other technologies are already reshaping how work is done.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is affecting hiring decisions, job design and workforce structures.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In this environment, the link between growth, jobs and skills is becoming less direct.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: He experiences it as one journey, from training to employment, to career and wage progression.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And the same is true from a business perspective.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A business does not think in terms of training policy versus employment policy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It thinks in terms of whether it can access the right skills, at the right time and at a cost it can sustain.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is where the rationale for the merger becomes clear.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It signals a shift towards a user-centric system, where support is organised around the journey of workers and the workforce needs of businesses, rather than around individual programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, the key question is how this translates into a better experience for businesses on the ground.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, companies today trying to reskill and redeploy workers must navigate multiple schemes, portals and processes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Even where support exists, it is not always clear how the different pieces fit together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs do not have the internal capacity to interpret policy intent, design training pathways and manage compliance across multiple schemes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In a fast-moving environment, these delays directly affect competitiveness and workforce outcomes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And beyond the front-end experience, how will the agency address the underlying system design?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Today, many programmes are designed to achieve similar outcomes but operate in parallel.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Even if access is streamlined, fragmentation can persist behind the scenes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A related point is preserving a strong employer focus.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While the merger brings jobs and skills together, the third leg is business demand, which ultimately generates those jobs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses are not just consumers of programmes; they are the source of job creation and the drivers of skills demand.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How will the agency ensure it remains deeply employer-responsive and not primarily programme-driven?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, how will it prioritise skills that employers need now rather than courses that are easier to scale or administer?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, while not suggesting further structural changes, it is important that the jobs and skills system remains closely anchored to enterprise transformation efforts led by Enterprise Singapore and supported by the trade associations and chambers (TACs), which are closest to business needs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A second area of responsiveness is sector-specific realities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Sustainability-focused sectors are adapting to new regulatory demands.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Feedback from the Singapore Manufacturing Federation suggests that sector-embedded models, such as the SkillsFuture Queen Bee approach, have been effective precisely because they are grounded in industry practice and supported by TACs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Even after the merger, it will be important to preserve and deepen this sector responsiveness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask how the agency intends to retain and strengthen sector-specific expertise.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Will industry-led frameworks, co-developed with TACs, continue to shape programme design?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And will support remain differentiated for SMEs and large enterprises, given that the majority of our workforce is employed by SMEs?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A third area is the funding and compliance framework.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
