text: But in recent years, the cumulative effect of tighter controls had been longer reimbursement timelines, heavier documentation requirements and increased administrative burden even for firms with strong track records.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For SMEs, this creates real cashflow strains, as firms often have to carry training and wage costs for extended periods while awaiting reimbursement.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Can we differentiate between employers with established compliance histories and higher-risk cases?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Can audits be more targeted and reliance placed more on post-disbursement or exception-based checks?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Related to this is how sensitive business information will be handled.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses understand the need for verification but may want clearer safeguards when requests touch on customer confidentiality, intellectual property or regulated information.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For many SMEs, the constraint is not access to training, but the ability to translate training into productivity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: What SMEs need is more applied support, contextualised training, embedded learning and project-based approaches tied to real operational challenges.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As AI accelerates, workforce disruption may become more frequent and more compressed in time.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: From a worker's perspective, the key issue is not just whether training is available, but how quickly that translates into re-employment.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How quickly and effectively workers are supported from displacement back into meaningful employment?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The use of integrated intelligence to identify at-risk workers earlier is a promising development.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How proactive will these interventions be in practice, and how will businesses be engaged when early signals of workforce disruption are identified?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, many firms would prefer to redesign roles and redeploy workers internally rather than retrench.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As the ecosystem of training, career and employment service providers expands, it will be important to ensure consistency in quality, standards and outcomes across providers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Many companies are already participating in ongoing programmes offered by WSG and SSG.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given the scale of integration, I would like to ask what further measures may be considered should issues persist beyond that period?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For SMEs in particular, delays in approvals or unclear responses can directly affect hiring, training and transformation decisions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It reflects the need for a more coordinated and integrated workforce system at a time when the pace of economic and technological change is accelerating.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we move into the next phase of transformation, the success of this merger will allow Singaporeans and our businesses to navigate a much more complex and uncertain future with confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But that itself, is only the means, it is not the end.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The real question is pretty simple: will this make life easier and clearer for Singaporeans trying to find their way in a changing economy?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my Budget speech, I spoke about transitions and the need to have greater clarity, and I think that is exactly the issue here that we are addressing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For many students, fresh graduates and workers today, the problem is not just whether support exists.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But both are really asking the same question: where does this path lead to?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And to me that is where SWDA comes in.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, if I may put it very bluntly and simply, SWDA must be the bridge between learning and work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a former educator, I have seen many students do everything right.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They study hard, they complete their courses, they submit their work, mostly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But as graduation approaches, many still become quite anxious.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Not because they do not want to start work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Not because they are not sure how to turn what they have learnt into a real first job.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Because they ask: fundamentally, does this qualification still matter?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will employers value me for what I can do?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Do I need experience before I can even get experience?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is what I would call the first-job gap.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is the gap between finishing a formative stage of life and seeing a real route towards meaningful work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is in that gap that confidence can disappear very quickly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I have seen capable, hardworking and promising students lose their footing at exactly the moment they should have been stepping forward with confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some took temporary work while trying to find their footing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some drifted into jobs beyond what they have been trained for, not because they chose that path confidently, but because they could not see a way into something better.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What they lacked was a clear bridge into work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And many parents are asking the same things in their own way: after all that effort, after all these years of study, is there a real pathway to a real job?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It helps fresh graduates gain experience and skills through structured traineeships and I find it very useful.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But it is still largely help that comes at a point after graduation and this issue is now even more urgent.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If one part of that is to help young people and fresh graduates find their footing, then that only reinforces the point that we cannot wait until the end of the journey to intervene.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When we talk about workforce development, we cannot wait until the end of the journey and then say: "Here are some portals, here are some schemes, good luck." That is not the pathway.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That means better career guidance earlier in the student's journey.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It means clearer signals on which jobs are growing and which skills matter.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It means making internships, attachments and industry projects more normal, not something enjoyed mainly by those who already have the right networks.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And it means making the school-to-work transition less dependent on luck.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our young people do not just need more options.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, some of them just graduated from their polytechnics and they messaged me about how happy they were to finish that line.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They shared, over time, that their challenge is really different.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For a CET learner, going back to class is rarely a small decision.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many are already working and they have family responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some are trying to recover from retrenchment, stagnation or simply a loss of confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, when a CET learner signs up for a course, normally, it is not casual.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are saying: I am willing to learn again.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am willing to put in the effort.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But I need to know this leads to somewhere.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is the gap between returning to learn and actually improving one's job prospects, income, confidence or long-term mobility, and this is where frustration can bite hard because many adult learners are not looking for enrichment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They do not want a certificate that just sits in a folder.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They want to know: will this help me pivot?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will this help me a role with prospects?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And will these skills that I have learnt be recognised?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I have taught adult learners who came to class after work, carrying family responsibilities and financial pressure, like I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They were serious, disciplined and were not there to collect papers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their question was always practical: if I invest my evenings, my weekends and my energy in this, will it really lead to better jobs, better wages, or a more secure future?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The issue in Singapore today is not just whether we have the courses.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not whether we have job vacancies.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is whether people can move from learning to work with greater confidence and less guesswork.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If SWDA works well, it can make that journey clearer, more practical and certainly, more credible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, make jobs and skills information far more usable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A student should be able to understand what jobs are growing, what adjacent roles exist and what skills employers value.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: An adult learner should be able to understand whether a course is likely to help with employability, a job move or a proper pivot.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Internships, attachments, project work and structured pathways into first jobs should not be left to chance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They should become more systematic, especially for those who do not already start with advantages.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Workers should be able to see what skills they already have, what roles they may be suited for, what gaps remain and what support can help them close that gap, and employers should be encouraged to hire with a clearer view of skills and potential, not just relying on pedigree shortcuts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is also where I think we can learn from what is already happening on the ground.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The issue is not which platform exists or which platform is better.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The issue is whether SWDA can make an overall experience more joined-up, so that workers do not feel like they are moving across separate islands of support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Fourth, support must arrive before the crisis, not after.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Too often, help comes after someone has already lost confidence, momentum or income.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We need a system that can identify risk earlier and support people while they still have time and options.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And frankly, that is a more humane policy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They experience it in much more simply, either I got help in time or I was left to figure it out by myself.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not enough to count how many people joined a particular programme, attended a course or received support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I think the real questions are: did they get a job?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Workers should be able to land, stay and progress.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If SWDA is bringing skills and employment together, then it should also bring measurements together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Otherwise, we may end up celebrating activity without knowing whether lives are actually improving.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay): In my work with M3+ Focus Area Four (FA4), and now as co-chair of the newly formed Economic Resilience Committee with Mr Saktiandi, it is clear to me that many Malay/Muslim youth, workers and families are not asking for sympathy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They want fair access to good jobs and real opportunities for advancement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this matters because each group requires a different form of support; youth who are just entering the workforce, fresh graduates seeking their first opportunity, mid-career workers who are adapting, professionals who want to remain relevant and entrepreneurs who want to continue to grow.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my work with M3+ FA4, this issue not just being studied at a policy level, but as a real effort to help job seekers and workers who are trying to adapt, upskill and regain their footing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In efforts such as the digital measures that we have launched, it also demonstrates that different groups require different kinds of support – youth as early adopters, families as users that need guidance, the workforce as practical users and seniors as users who need to be reassured.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What matters now is ensuring that this confidence translates into good jobs, career advancement and economic resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We have made progress in education and training.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But for many Malay/Muslim families, the real question is whether the pathway is clear for them?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Clear from unstable work to a better career.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is where the role of SWDA must truly be felt on the ground.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As part of the efforts by FA4 effort as well as the Economic Resilience Committee, I hope we can work closely with SWDA so that the support provided truly matches the needs of different groups: whether they are youth, fresh graduates, mid-career workers, professionals and entrepreneurs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This includes identifying growth sectors with strong potential, connecting our community to those opportunities, and building pathways that can genuinely translate into good jobs, career advancement and long-term economic resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For me, this is not merely a matter of access.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Sir, if SWDA succeeds, our PET students will step into work with greater confidence, our CET learners will have greater assurance that learning can lead to real progress and our workers will move faster into suitable roles with less confusion and less anxiety.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One of the ways that our policies seek to do so is by getting workers to undertake further training and education.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Attending courses, often whilst juggling work and other life commitments, requires a significant expenditure of energy, time and also money.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As we debate the merger of SSG and WSG into the SWDA, we must ensure that processes and policies instituted in the new agency are ultimately rooted in people, a people-centric approach.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They must lead to fruitful employment opportunities for workers and result in a deep pool of talent for employers to draw from.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A people-centric approach to skills upgrading should also be easy for training providers to navigate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, given that institutions would have to satisfy both academic standards and industrial needs, can the Minister clarify what would be the new agency's approach should there be any tension between these two aims?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, how do we resolve competing aims that may arise out of the short-term workforce needs of industry against a longer-term educational and development lens?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How will we end up preventing the creation of a two-headed monster in this new agency?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Specifically, what safeguards will we put in place to prevent fragmented oversight or conflicting directives within the agency?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another crucial aspect of a people-centred SWDA is to ensure open availability of granular information for the public and policy-makers alike to analyse the outcome of the agency's policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is established under clause 5(1)(g), which articulates the agency's responsibility to collect and publish data on career, employment and training matters alongside labour market insights.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Do we have data that shows that the opportunities matched and employment secured via these services do match jobseeker skills and qualifications?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Effective job matching requires career advisers with wide networks and a deep understanding of their industry.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What is the Minister's assessment of the Volunteer Career Adviser Scheme's effectiveness in job matching and what are the Government's future plans regarding the scheme?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Drilling down further into our existing programmes, the Career Conversion Programme and GRIT programme are aimed at mid-career workers and fresh graduates respectively.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In addition to providing work experience, these programmes also provide participants a pathway towards full-time employment with their host organisation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How do we ensure that employers are not exploiting these schemes as a revolving door of Government-subsidised labour, instead of meaningfully inducting participants into full-time roles in their host organisations after the programme is completed?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Although retention data is available at the industry level via Parliamentary Questions, it would be informative to study the proportion of participants retained as full-time employees by their respective host organisations at the employer level, including how long such employees stayed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As mentioned by my Sengkang colleague, Jamus Lim, during Committee of Supply this year, we could allow a maximum number of times for an employer to participate in a programme but not employ any trainees upon completion of the programme.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could be a start to help us identify if there are employers who may be exploiting such schemes for cheaper labour, ultimately running counter to the spirit of such programmes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There was also a rush by many Singaporeans to redeem their expiring SkillsFuture credits last year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet were these credits utilised for courses and programmes that genuinely improved our people's employability or offer positive contributions to personal growth and development that trickle into other dive domains?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A Forum letter to The Straits Times at the end of last year voiced a concern about the quality of some SkillsFuture courses – overpriced, with poor learning outcomes and laughable assessments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, such self-reported surveys may not accurately reflect the effectiveness of these courses in enhancing the employment prospects of their attendees.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To measure employment outcomes, we need to focus more on objective metrics, such as longer-term post-course employment status, in order to more accurately evaluate whether these courses genuinely improve employment outcomes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This analysis could be carried out, for example, using Central Provident Fund (CPF) data to determine the effectiveness of each SkillsFuture course.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it can be argued that having these schemes are reflective of a government willing to invest in building the capabilities of its people, the jury is still out on their return on investment without sufficient data publicly available.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having public data allows the public to know about the effectiveness of their schemes and will aid to pinpoint potential areas for improvement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also, while the Government is an active creator of early career opportunities, such as internships and traineeships, I also hope that we can work towards providing more opportunities for mid-career transitioners as well.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would also like to make a few remarks on how we develop a significant part of our workforce – persons with disabilities (PwDs).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we wish to see the greater integration of PwDs into the wider community, the targets we set must encompass a wider range of factors.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While skill and qualification-related underemployment within the overall labour market was tracked in a recent NTUC study on underemployment, the Disabled People's Association (DPA) suggested in 2024 that these metrics should also be tracked for the PwD community.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Coordination with SG Enable needs to take place to collect and publish data surrounding the retention of participants under the School-To-Work and Place-and-Train programmes to ensure these programmes' effectiveness and boosting full-time employment amongst PwDs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As many job seekers with disabilities experience demoralising hurdles when job hunting, a people-centric and inclusive SWDA should be attuned to the needs of PwDs, thus helping to address under employment among PwDs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Interviews with PwDs by the DPA also highlighted the tendency for jobseekers with disabilities to be pigeonholed into certain roles, especially within the services industry.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we wish for PwDs to thrive in our society, they should not be constrained to a select few job scopes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that the SWDA would factor in the prior skills and experience of jobseekers with disabilities when job matching.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additional support could be regarded via an in-house accessibility office, which could provide services, such as consulting with employers regarding reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must additionally ensure that PwDs have fewer barriers to access the wide range of courses available for re-skilling and upskilling.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is in alignment with Article 27 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which calls on governments to enable PwDs' effective access to general technical and vocational guidance programmes, placement services and vocational and continuing training.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Enabling Academy's work in developing training courses catered to PwDs on topics, such as AI and cooking, is important, in the spirit of inclusivity, SkillsFuture courses should be made accessible to all via the provision of reasonable accommodations, a point that I and others in this House have previously made.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During the recent Budget Statement, the Prime Minister highlighted the outsized role AI plays in our economic strategy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, the recently updated criteria for courses to obtain Government funding requires either certification from a course endorsement body, or 50% of the skills taught should be listed on the Course Approval Skills List (CASL).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For the CASL, in particular, the skills listed support good growth jobs and are important for Singapore's economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While skills important to the social sector, such as social services, youth development and casework management, are included in the CASL, I believe we can do more to drive up our social service manpower capacity and overall interest in the sector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I previously mentioned in my Budget 2024 speech, I hope that the agency would platform these skills in addition to economic growth drivers, such as tech and AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, while the SWDA drives economic growth by widening and deepening our talent pool, the agency work also affects the livelihoods of individual Singaporeans, and we must ensure that it is people centric.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This involves untangling unnecessary red tape for training providers and broadening the types of data collected to monitor the agency's effectiveness in securing fruitful employment opportunities and outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, the agency should also boost its capabilities serving marginalised communities, such as PwDs and ex-offenders, whilst promoting the people sector, not just focus on areas with strong economic potential.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Jobs are being redesigned, new roles are emerging and existing roles are evolving at a faster pace than ever before.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For many workers, especially mid-career and lower-wage workers, these changes bring both opportunity and uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In this context, the need for a more integrated and responsive workforce development system is clear.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Skills acquisition, employment and progression are closely interlinked.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Bringing these functions together within a single agency can reduce fragmentation and improve coordination.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For workers, this should mean a more seamless experience, where access to career guidance, training and job placements are better aligned.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As this integration is implemented, it will be important to ensure that processes remain streamlined and responsive to both workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In particular, we must ensure that this more integrated system delivers for those who need it most.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They often face greater constraints in accessing training and career opportunities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The system must therefore be designed with their needs in mind.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It should be accessible, adequately supported and outcome-focused, so that workers can upgrade without undue strain and see clear improvements in employment and wages.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: PWM has uplifted lower-wage workers by linking wages to skills, productivity and career progression.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It has also contributed to sustained wage growth across several sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For PWM to remain effective, it must be supported by a well-aligned skills ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, I encourage continued collaboration with tripartite partners to keep sectoral skills frameworks current and responsive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Third, I call on the new agency to expand workplace-based training, enabling workers to upgrade while remaining employed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At the same time, sustained wage growth depends on continued productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can it provide more structured advisory support, practical tools and targeted funding to help companies adopt technology and better match skills to jobs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will be key to ensuring that productivity keeps pace with wage increases and that PWM remains sustainable over the long term.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Building on this link between skills and progression, let me turn to the Careers and Skills Passport that was introduced in 2024 and also mentioned by the Minister in his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This initiative can complement PWM, particularly in sectors where wage progression is tied to clearly defined skills ladders.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The passport provides workers with a consolidated record of their skills and experience, improving both transparency and portability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, one key question is whether lower-wage workers, especially those in PWM sectors, are actively using the passport today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If not, what more can be done to raise awareness, improve accessibility and encourage adoption among this group?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must ensure that tools, like the Careers and Skills Passport, are not just used by those who are already ahead, but also by those we most want to uplift.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How does the new agency plan to integrate the passport with sectoral skills frameworks, particularly in PWM sectors?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And how will it support employers, especially SMEs, to use the passport more effectively in hiring and progression decisions?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Stronger and more inclusive adoption can improve skills recognition and job matching outcomes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond supporting workers in employment and progression, we must also ensure that those who step out of the workforce can return with confidence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As I have previously highlighted in this House, returning to work after an injury or an illness is often not straightforward.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Workers may face reduced capacity, loss of confidence and uncertainty about how to re-enter employment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A setback in health should not become a permanent setback in employment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At the same time, employers may be unsure how best to accommodate such workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Recovery is not just a medical issue, it is also a workplace issue.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We therefore need a more structured and coordinated approach.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Jobs must adapt to workers, just as workers adapt to jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can the new agency work more closely with employers to redesign roles and identify suitable job opportunities?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How will the new agency support targeted training and career guidance to help these workers re-enter the workforce?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A phased return to work can make the difference between dropping out and staying in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More broadly, we must move from ad hoc support to a structured return-to-work system, so that workers are not left behind due to unforeseen life circumstances.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we keep these outcomes at the centre of our efforts, this reform will strengthen both our workforce system and the compact between workers, employers and the Government.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, we are asked today to approve the merger of two agencies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I would use this occasion to ask whether the system they inherit is the right one.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We often speak of skills upgrading and credentials.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The real question is simpler: are we building real capabilities for our workers?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Here is where I think the Government has done well.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the biggest gains went to non-PMET and mature workers – the groups the credit-based system has struggled to reach.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I also would like to acknowledge the 38 Skills Frameworks that were co-built with industry, unions and professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They are a useful compilation of the skills and competencies expected for each role in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But as those who have been hiring managers know: what is in the frameworks sets necessary but insufficient bars.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: You still need interviews and competency tests to actually hire well.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This success of this Place-and-Train employer-anchored programme contrasts with other parts of the system which are not doing so well, such as the credit-based, individual-based SkillsFuture programme.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The credit-based side of the system has struggled on both integrity and take-up.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2017, a syndicate fraud extracted nearly $40 million through fake enrolments.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Auditor-General later found millions more in overpayments and uncollected levies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I do not think this is an execution failure, but a flaw in the policy idea itself.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The SkillsFuture system of the last decade is an example of the individual-credit system: the Government funds individuals to purchase courses from a permissive provider market.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Suppliers capture the funds; fraud is possible; links with entry-level capability are weak.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The largest meta-analysis of active labour-market programmes – Card, Kluve and Weber, 2018, with 207 estimates across 200-plus studies – found classroom training shows weak or negative short-run effects, with gains emerging only at the two- to three-year mark, and concentrated on the long-term unemployed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The populations best served by these programmes are the displaced and long-term jobless, not mid-career workers who need to shore up against job precarity or climb the wage ladder.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2015, under President Hollande, they launched the Compte Personnel de Formation, a personal training account.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Training hours attached to the person, not the job.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The 2018 Macron reform converted those hours to euros – €500 a year, capped at €5,000, with higher caps for the lower-qualified.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Then, in 2019 they built an app, Mon Compte Formation, a consumer-grade marketplace where any worker could browse, book or pay for any accredited course in a few taps.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Employers and unions were disintermediated and cut out entirely.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: More than two million training purchases a year.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It was one of the boldest individual-credit experiments of any major economy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Cold callers and fictitious providers followed the money.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: France spent the next four years walking it back: banning cold-calling, imposing co-payments that have since been raised twice, capping the most-abused course categories.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: France had the digital infrastructure, had the regulators and had the financial intelligence unit.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What it did not have was any party other than the state itself bearing consequences for training quality.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The principal-agent problem is not solved by transparency, digitisation or individual choice.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The chain of transmission of consequences for an individual credit system, from Ministry to agency to provider to learner to employer, is such that nobody bears the consequences of low-quality training.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Career Conversion Programmes work because an employer is the principal before training begins.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The individual-credit channel, by design, lacks that principal and no amount of enforcement can substitute for it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It seems SkillsFuture has unfolded in a similar way.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Can we redesign the system so that employers, not individuals purchasing courses, become the accountable parties?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Not individual choice, which is what we have, but structured employer accountability: sectoral associations and firms bearing reputational and financial consequences for training quality.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Employers with skin in the game will push for a fuller accounting of what a job actually requires, not just entry criteria, but the tacit knowledge needed to stay and grow.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When funds are provisioned individually, the government defaults to input-side accountability: ensuring providers are accredited, claims meet thresholds and participants receive a certification.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Whether the credential improves a worker's employability is not measurable at the point of purchase, only in labour outcomes, years later.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The system optimises for what it can count, not what it should produce.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I think it is desirable to have sectoral associations and firms lead the upskilling journey directly to solve the principal-agent problem and consequently, invest in deep, long-duration training.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How do other economies solve the principal-agent problem?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Germany's apprenticeship system operates within one of Europe's most mobile credentialed labour markets, their Industrie- und Handelskammer or Chambers of Industry and Commerce certification is portable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The goal is workers who are chosen repeatedly at a premium, not workers who cannot leave.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Economic skill-formation literature identifies three conditions for firms to invest in deep, long-duration training.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, industry co-governance of curriculum – so that what is taught tracks what industry actually needs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Industry transformation maps and trade associations do consultative work that touches co-governance, but it is advisory, not binding – no sectoral employer body exercises a sign-off or veto on SkillsFuture curriculum, and no named individual's reputation moves with and is staked on the employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: As I understand it, NTUC mainly bargains at the enterprise level rather than at the collective sector level.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, I think we have neither true industry co-governance of curriculums, nor do we have sectoral bargaining to achieve wage compression.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some will say Singapore is too small for German-style sectoral institutions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Switzerland, population nine million, sustains deep sectoral bargaining and apprenticeship in pharma, watchmaking and machine tools.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: NTUC's current architecture is attuned to individual employer engagement.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is not the right vehicle for deep tacit-knowledge sectors.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These sectors need binding sectoral wage scales, not just floors, but scales that compress the wage distribution.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Right now, a firm that invests in deep training risks losing that worker to a competitor the day after certification.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It narrows pay gaps so poaching is not worth it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The return on training stays with the firm that trained.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is why German firms fund three-year apprenticeships at their own expense.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The PWM lifts wages for lower-wage workers, and it does so well.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It says to the worker: train, and you move up.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What we need is a structure that says to the employer: train deeply, because you will keep the return.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Sectoral bargaining fits sectors with deep tacit knowledge – semiconductor backend, aerospace MRO, petrochemicals, marine and offshore – but perhaps not faster-moving industries like AI.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Named industry entities and individuals should have sign-off and veto on SkillsFuture curricula, not as advisors, but as accountable parties whose reputations move with employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We must also lower the accreditation barriers that keep the most credible practitioners out.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For faster-moving industries – AI, software, frontier hardware – the fixes above may not work.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Skills change too fast; firms are too few and too mobile.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What works in these sectors is something different: knowledge spreading through people working near each other.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is how Shenzhen and Silicon Valley were built – rapid knowledge diffusion through firms, suppliers and people solving problems together, carrying what they learned into the next job.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We cannot build a Shenzhen-scale agglomeration on 750 square kilometres.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: One, engineer knowledge diffusion through people, not papers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To produce an industrial commons here, first, we will need to revive the engineering society ethos.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we are serious about capability over credentials, the most basic question is: do our workers and engineers know how things work?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We need to know how things work at the level of teardown and re-assembly because that is the foundation of any serious industrial capability.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The model is Munro and Associates in Michigan, which has spent close to four decades disassembling competitor vehicles down to the last fastener and producing the detailed cost, design and process reports that the global automotive industry treats as authoritative.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Japan's National Institutes of Technology teach 15-year-olds to disassemble electromechanical systems in formal "Reverse Engineering" courses.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The US military reverse-engineered the Iranian Shahed drone and fielded its own version in Venezuela at $35,000 per unit, versus $1.3 million for a Tomahawk cruise missile.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Understanding how things are built is not a hobby.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should reverse-engineer frontier hardware – electric vehicles, batteries, solar, drones.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Structured public reports should feed the industrial commons.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Such facilities could also be housed at A*STAR's centres, which I understand already runs model factories and joint industry labs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Partnered with ITEs and polytechnics, with structured access for SMEs, they would form a strong starting point.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For ordinary citizens, the National Library Board's MakeIT at Libraries – its free maker-space programme run with the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), offering 3D printing, digital cutting, robotics and coding classes in selected regional libraries – teaches the basics well.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I have observed 3D printing and robotics classes there, and the starter sessions are well-designed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But the curriculum stops there, with no intermediate or advanced progression.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we are serious about life-long learning, MakeIT needs a vertical curriculum – Stage 2 and Stage 3 modules, project-based, progressing from operating the machines to designing with them and using them more intensely – not just a wider menu of first lessons.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Knowledge does not diffuse simply because firms share a postcode.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Tacit production knowledge – the working understanding of why a process line behaves the way it does, what failure modes to watch for, which suppliers to trust – does not transfer through papers or seminars.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It transfers through people, on the floor, over months.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Engineer circulation, not patents or licensing, was the primary transmission mechanism.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We can do this as a pilot in the tacit-knowledge sectors I named earlier – semiconductor backend, aerospace MRO, petrochemicals, marine and offshore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we want an industrial commons, we must make the people circulate.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Teacher rotation through industry should also try to be a statutory requirement.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is the first task: making the knowledge already inside Singapore circulate.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The second task is to go to where the knowledge is being created.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Overseas Markets Immersion Programme (OMIP), launched in 2024, is the right vehicle in form.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Salary support of up to 70% for nine months, capped at $5,000 a month, with a minimum salary threshold of $4,000 a month effectively restricts it to PMETs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If I had to name one programme that could be reframed tomorrow at low cost and high return, it is OMIP.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, remove the minimum salary threshold for technical and operational roles in priority sectors, so ITE-trained engineers and polytechnic graduates can be deployed to cutting-edge manufacturing clusters in China, Japan and Europe – not only PMETs in regional roles.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: OMIP is currently designed as outbound business development support – helping Singapore companies expand into new markets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It should also be inbound knowledge acquisition – sending Singaporeans to where manufacturing knowledge is being created, to bring it back.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The architecture is broad enough to hold both, if we choose to use it that way.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The deepest lesson of the last decade of skills policy, here and abroad, is this: the state cannot substitute for the firm as the principal in a worker's training.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have spent 10 years and considerable public money trying.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The next 10 years should be spent designing the system in which sectors and firms – and the workers themselves, through their unions – are forced to care about the answer.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And an order-of-magnitude expansion of how we send Singaporeans to where cutting-edge knowledge actually lives.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It deepens inside sectors and firms, which is why we need sectoral architecture that holds workers there long enough for it to form.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And it circulates through an industrial commons – which is why we need engineers, instructors, and Singaporeans abroad moving through that commons, carrying knowledge with them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The state is an orchestrator, it builds the architecture in which both happen.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In the PME who has just been made redundant, in the fresh graduate sending out applications that go unanswered, in the 58-year-old who wonders if anyone will hire him again, in the caregiver who stepped away for five years now does not know how to step back in.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: It is the right thing to do for every Singaporean worker.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: But here is the truth: learning and working are not two separate journeys.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: When these two functions live in separate houses, workers and jobseekers fall through the gaps between them.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They complete a course and find no pathway to a job.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They get placed in a job with no support to grow.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For many workers, it felt like a maze.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: It signals that a course without a career pathway is incomplete and a job placement without skills development is unsustainable.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We have counted the number of courses taken, credits used, certificates earned.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: While those numbers matter, they are not the finish line.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The finish line is this: did training lead to a better job?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: A worker who feels more secure, more valued, more able to provide for their family?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Because if a worker sacrifices evenings and weekends to attend training, pushes through self-doubt and emerges with a certificate that leads nowhere or worse, leads to a job that pays the same, or continues receiving job application rejections as before, then we have failed them.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The training system has taken their time, resources and their hope but have returned nothing of real value.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The new agency's mandate must be clear: measure outcomes, not just outputs.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Progression to a higher-value role, not a lateral transfer, not a downgrade.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: A worker with the dignity of a career that moves forward and upwards.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Course accreditation must no longer ask only if this course is well-designed?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: It must ask: does this course lead to real employment and real outcomes?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Does it lead to wage and career progression?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Is it connected to industries that are hiring, and hiring at fair wages?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The merged agency now has access to both SSG's training ecosystem and WSG's employment data.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: It can see both sides of the equation.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: And to employers, I say this directly: the social compact must be both ways.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: When a worker reskills, their wage, the title must reflect that upgrade.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Visible, searchable, accountable – these indicators will help to keep the system honest.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The SkillsFuture Queen Bee initiative, working alongside NTUC's Company Training Committees, has delivered real results.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: At ST Engineering, jobs were redesigned, workers were upgraded, productivity improved.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Many SMEs are not plugged into these ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This is why SWDA should leverage the upcoming Tripartite Jobs Council more as a greater partner than just a consultative forum.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: It should see the Tripartite Jobs Council as a driver on the ground coordination amidst all this AI disruption, to bring about sector-wide transformation so that good jobs and sustained careers reach whole industries and not just flagship firms.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: SWDA should see the advantages of tapping on the strengths of tripartite partners like NTUC and the Singapore National Employers Federation to reach the employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: It grounds the agency in reality whether training leads to real jobs, whether transitions are navigable, whether policies reflect what happens in the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For mid-career workers, the new agency must be a lifeline.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Income support, skills training and job placement must be delivered as a package and not patchwork.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: A worker who needs six months to reskill cannot survive on willpower alone.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: And at the end of that journey, there must be a job waiting.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For senior workers above 50, we must be honest.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The new agency must not just train senior workers, it must work aggressively with employers to shift mindsets.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Senior workers bring institutional knowledge, emotional intelligence and resilience that no algorithm can replicate.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They must be placed in roles that honour their experience and not sidelined beneath their capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For lower-income workers and those without degrees: the SkillsFuture movement has always risked being captured by the already-advantaged.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The new agency must reach down to these workers, not wait for them to come to the agency.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Community outreach, vernacular language support, simplified processes and critically, training pathways that lead to genuine wage progression because they have the most to gain.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For young people from ITE and polytechnics, do not assume that they have it easy.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Many feel invisible in a system that celebrates degrees.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: But what matters more is that every Singaporean who walks into a career centre, logs onto a portal or calls a helpline feels seen, feels that someone genuinely is in their corner, not to tick a box, but to walk with them until they reach a better place.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: These officers have built deep expertise, they are not just assets to be reorganised, they are the people who will deliver this transformation.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They deserve clarity, investment and pathways to grow alongside the agency that they are building.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Because better training must lead to better jobs.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: And better wages must lead to better lives for every Singaporean, without an exception.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It reflects a deeper shift in how we think about jobs, skills and careers in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At its core, this Bill recognises a structural reality, that skills development and employment outcomes can no longer be treated as separate policy domains.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, training and employment must connect more tightly, not only in policy design, but in how Singaporeans experience the system.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is a deliberate move towards a more integrated, end-to-end workforce system.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In the next decade, we should be measuring success by not how many courses a worker attends but how many transitions are completed into good jobs with progression.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Today, training and employment are delivered by separate agencies and both have done commendable work.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Skills are acquired, but jobs may not follow.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Workers may complete courses without clear pathways into employment.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, employers may report difficulty finding job-ready talent.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Some residents have shared these concerns with me.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are middle-aged, mid-career PMETs who have lost their jobs.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They used their SkillsFuture subsidies and trained in areas like AI, data analysis and project management.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Yet despite their efforts, they still find it difficult to secure work that is commensurate with their skills and seniority.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Some have also shared that while they are prepared to learn, they are less clear about what a realistic entry point looks like when moving into a brand new sector.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When some mid-career workers used SkillsFuture to take courses in high demand areas like AI, data or project management, product management, they may understandably hope to re-enter at the same level of seniority and remuneration they previously held.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But in practice, they are competing with candidates who already have track records in these sectors and employers may be hiring for proven experience, not only course completion.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When outcomes do not match expectations, some become discouraged, disgruntled and conclude that their training did not work even though the real barrier may be the entry point into a new industry.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This raises a policy question for the new agency.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because the citizens advice and expectations differ in each case.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If we try to signal both at once, we risk sending mixed messages and confusing citizens at the very point that they seek and need clarity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I therefore suggest that the new agency consider finetuning SkillsFuture into clearer pathways.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One pathway could focus on sector entry and conversion with transparent expectations on likely starting roles, salary ranges and the additional steps needed beyond courses, such as supervised projects, apprenticeship or structured workplace attachments.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Another pathway could then focus on progression for those who are already in the sector where SkillsFuture support deeper specialisation and advancement of skills.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This distinction will make the citizen journey clearer and help training translate more reliable into hiring outcomes.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, the key issue here is not willingness of the individual.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The linkage between training choices, employer recognition and hiring outcomes.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Courses build capability but pathways will build confidence.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The new agency presents an opportunity to close this gap.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It can move us towards a system where training is not only supply-driven but aligned to real labour market demand.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And it can make pathways clearer at the point where a worker must decide what he must do, he or she must do next.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Every Singaporean who invests his time and effort into upgrading should see a meaningful return, in real employment opportunity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many Singaporeans may have to reskill and pivot multiple times in their career.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, workforce support cannot be activated only when one loses a job or signs up for a course.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Some workers may also need more flexible routes to sustain household income during these transition phases, including fractional work arrangements or micro-entrepreneurship, where appropriate.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But for many, the barrier is not motivation.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The formation of this new agency provides an opportunity to move in that direction.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With a unified view of skills and employment data, the agency can offer more proactive, tailored and personalised support.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It can identify at-risk workers earlier, guide them towards the relevant training and support smoother transitions into new roles.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, I seek clarification on how the agency intends to balance standardisation and customisation.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A centralised and standardised system of course can achieve efficiency.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But it must remain responsive to diverse needs.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This includes mid-career professionals, lower-wage workers, gig workers, those in emerging sectors and those returning to work after caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In other words, Mr Speaker, Sir, the system must be integrated, but it cannot become impersonal.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Singapore has achieved high participation in training programmes.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But participation alone does not necessarily translate into equitable outcomes.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must ensure the benefits of this integrated system are accessible to all, especially those who need it most.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This includes lower-income workers, those with lower educational attainment and workers in sectors undergoing disruption.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Equity is not just about access to training.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is also about whether the system is navigable for those with the least time, least confidence and least support.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We should also recognise a practical constraint here.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Moreover, a number of disadvantaged Singaporeans work beyond their main jobs to supplement household incomes.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because if the system is seamless only for those already in advantaged positions, then it truly is not seamless.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It shifts us from separate interventions towards a more integrated, continuous and responsive system.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But integration cannot be just WSG and SSG shaking hands.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our residents must feel that their hands are held throughout the employment journey.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With these comments, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It will also improve the user experience for workers and jobseekers who tap on the two agencies' funding and online resources for their skills and career development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, enterprises that receive public funding for skills and workforce development will have a more seamless interface with the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: With significant workforce disruption on the horizon, the formation of SWDA would strengthen the ecosystem of support for workers to reskill and invest in their career health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding, there are several points I would like to seek the Minister's clarification on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Since the launch of the SkillsFuture movement in 2015, the IHLs have pivoted from focusing mainly on PET to also embracing CET, building up their CET course offerings and becoming partners in lifelong learning for their students and graduates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While Singapore's lifelong learning efforts must support employability, there are other objectives as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Besides working adults, retirees too must be encouraged to continue learning to keep their minds supple and engaged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I would like to clarify whether SWDA will actively promote lifelong learning that is not targeted at employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Will the agency give sufficient attention to the broader aims of lifelong learning as well, particularly given Singapore's growing senior population?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: With the formation of SWDA, there is opportunity to merge or streamline the myskillsfuture and mycareersfuture online portals for a more seamless user journey for those looking to reskill for new jobs and careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is investing considerable resources in training and reskilling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This gives substance to the creed that every worker matters, and to the commitment that every worker who wishes to will be supported to reskill for new jobs and careers, even as technology transforms work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, it is important to ensure that public money is well spent – and this is a point that many in the House have raised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: First, while the Bill addresses abusive funding arrangements and false or misleading advertisements, including setting out penalties and remedial measures, I would like to ask if the Ministry could elaborate on the steps that will be taken to reduce the risk of fraud or abuse of grants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, will SWDA monitor how skills acquired through training are deployed at the workplace and assess their impact on employment outcomes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It may be timely for a systematic evaluation of the various SSG and WSG programmes to determine which ought to be scaled up and conversely, which ought to be scaled back or discontinued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: On training grants, funding for WSQ courses is based on the number of trainees who successfully complete and pass the course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While training providers should select students carefully and equip them to succeed, it is to be expected that a small number of trainees will fail to complete or pass the course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important to avoid a situation where because of financial considerations, there is pressure on adult educators to do no more than teach to the test or even pass students who in fact do not make the mark.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, could training providers be compensated for trainees who do not manage to pass the course – say up to five or 10% of a class – since the training providers would have incurred costs for these trainees?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In this era of rapid change, training and learning must be nimble and responsive to changing market needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Training providers may need a "fail fast, learn fast" approach in launching new courses or experimenting with new teaching methods or technologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: How will SWDA ensure timely course approval, balancing quality considerations with the need for speed in mounting new courses or updating curricula in response to changing technology and job demands?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While a certain risk tolerance is needed for innovation and agility, funding should also reward impact and steer support towards training that proves effective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, are there plans to review grant structure and KPIs to incentivise desired outcomes from training, beyond training placement and completion rates?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, workers must take responsibility in planning for their career and skills development needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: They must invest proactively in career health and not just act when their jobs and livelihoods are at imminent risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: How then can SWDA help to foster agency in individuals to do so?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: What new approaches, if any, will the agency take in engaging workers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: For learning to bring tangible benefit to enterprises and organisations, it must move beyond episodic programmes and courses to become deeply embedded in organisational strategy and DNA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Data from the OECD's Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies suggest that for innovation-intensive workplaces, non-formal and informal learning are most prevalent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Formal training must therefore be complemented and integrated with workplace learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, how can SWDA help enterprises become learning organisations where there is strong alignment between business strategy and people strategy, and where learning takes place in the flow of work?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Can learning at work be codified and skills recognised to facilitate portability, such as through portfolio-based recognition or skills credentialling?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: How does SWDA plan to scale impact across the large number of SMEs in different industries that need support?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This House will shortly debate a Motion on an AI Transition with No Jobless Growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The future of work and the human contribution to work are fundamental to Singapore's social compact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: How can Singapore build up expertise in human-centric job redesign so that wherever possible, AI will augment rather than replace human capabilities?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: How can SWDA help organisations build capability in job redesign and workplace learning?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It also helps employers tap on a wider pool of talent and utilise employee skills more fully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Institute for Adult Learning, as the national centre of excellence in adult learning, stands ready to support SWDA in this important work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: What is at stake is nothing less than Singapore's work-based social compact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: And for this reason, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We steward more than 1,000 livelihoods and interact with Government agencies on workforce development initiatives.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Thankfully, I am from the Party that uses lightning as a symbol and we are not afraid of storms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: There are also other storms in the world today.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And this Bill provides for a change that is an appropriate response to inexorable trends from these storms, trends that I highlighted in my maiden Parliamentary speech – that the technology cycle has shortened significantly and therefore, skills are becoming obsolete faster.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, we are living longer.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: If you combine these two trends, the natural conclusion is that the traditional "learn, work, retire" trajectory is a relic of the past.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: A young Singaporean today may have to navigate a 50-year career spanning multiple companies and perhaps, quite possibly multiple industries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We can, therefore, no longer rely on what we learnt in pre-employment training to carry us through to retirement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, there may even come a point in time that we learnt in the first year of tertiary education will become irrelevant by the time we graduate.
