speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We see this manifest in greater anxieties across the workforce, especially on the faces of new graduates and older PMETs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I have spoken to many in Jalan Besar and Whampoa-Boon Keng and I feel for them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a clear direction, given that SSG and all of its resources would effectively be moving from MOE to MOM.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But I also hope we will retain some of the strengths of the earlier model at MOE, which developed a strong nexus between our IHLs and the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: MOE could and should maintain some level of oversight and accountability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, the Government should consider appointing one of our MOE political officeholders to have a secondary role at MOM.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I am sure the Minister for Manpower would welcome that extra help.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The longer-term question is how to redirect more of our limited resources and efforts towards continuing education and training.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We have to move away from the mindset that a degree or a diploma is the be-all and end-all of learning.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, it is but the start of a lifetime of acquiring and applying new skills.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I sometimes wonder why we need to cram so much knowledge into our students before they join the workforce.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Is it not better to provide a shorter duration of pre-employment training and to redirect more resources to mid-career training programmes?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I have also mentioned in Parliament before about the need to be more focussed with our Government-funded programmes to move away from SkillsFuture programmes that are unlikely to lead to employment which, in my mind, is not an effective use of the Government's resources.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We all have residents who tell us that they attend SkillsFuture courses, thinking that they would find jobs, only to be bitterly disappointed.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: As many Members of Parliament, like Dr Wan Rizal said, we do not want a situation where Singaporeans are spending time and effort to learn skills that employers simply do not want.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is therefore better to put these resources into the hands of those who are most likely to know which skills are valued.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: These are the employers who compete daily in the marketplace to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: They are our best bet to forward-sense the demand signals of a constantly changing market.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: These are also our trade associations and our unions, who are able to aggregate demand across multiple employers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, Mr Kenneth Tiong also spoke about trade associations and accrediting training.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We should move away from short-term SkillsFuture courses that do not have good employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: By helping companies to hire workers first and then train them on the job, the skills being taught are immediately relevant and utilised for both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And in a world where younger workers may find themselves irrelevant, we should not discriminate against long-term jobseekers by age.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And as a final point, just as we want employers and employees to be adaptable and agile, I hope the SWDA will, likewise, be the same.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The agency must be adaptable enough to embrace the uncertainty that we cannot possibly know which skills are in demand in the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The agency must also be agile enough to work within a changing landscape of partners, such as the e2i and the new Tripartite Jobs Council, for the delivery of programmes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that MOM can also clarify how there will be synergies and not a duplication of programmes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Overall, as many other Members have said, the success of the SWDA will depend on how we can structure the right incentives and measure the right outcomes.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: As a practising engineer and an active educator, I have dedicated my career to the mastery of professional skills and the transfer of industry relevant knowledge to the workforce or through the CET programmes.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I have been in CET training for more than 10 years and I am honoured to be awarded the SkillsFuture Fellowship in 2023.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: For many specialised roles, a certificate of completion is not sufficient.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: My industry, like engineering or the built environment, and cybersecurity, all the industries that basically operate on a system of professional accreditation.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In these sectors, specific jobs require certified training and accumulated experience that then result in formal industry recognition.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Without this, even the most hardworking worker may find their career progression stalled because they lack the "professional currency" for higher-tier employment.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: That means that for the new agency, collaborations or the integration of the career pathway of professionals will be very important in the skills training.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Professional institutions, whether it is accounting or corporate secretaries or insurance, they have well-defined pathway for career progression based on expertise and experience, or capabilities and competencies.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Our employers recognise such industrial accreditation and certification for their skills mastery.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: As a SkillsFuture Fellow and a trainer, I have seen many talented individuals pick up different skillsets, maybe a little bit haphazardly, but struggle to have these skills "counted" toward the professional titles.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, in engineering or in the Institution of Engineers, Singapore, we have three tiers – from chartered technicians to chartered technologists, to chartered engineers.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Depending on the academic level, you enter at different stages, then you can continue to progress based on the experience you acquire and also the course and skills mastery that you achieve.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It is not necessary for you to get a degree in order to become a chartered engineer.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: You can actually progress through your skills mastery through experience and expertise.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, let me give an example – we have chartered engineers in system engineering and we can have chartered technicians in railway.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: By closely integrating the link between training and professional accreditation, we will provide our workforce with more than just knowledge.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We provide them with a recognised professional career pathway.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is clear that our workforce faces significant challenges today.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In the recent Committee of Supply debate on manpower, I highlighted the critical need to refresh our career and employment services ecosystem and the need for a new compact among all the stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I also noted the critical role of the Government.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Government is uniquely positioned to identify emerging trends, anticipate disruptions and take a macro helicopter view.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This perspective allows it to connect the dots across education, training and employment, and to align stakeholders to the evolving needs of our economy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There is no better time to ask some hard questions.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: What is the mission of this new agency?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: What are the metrics and the KPIs that we are measuring success with?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: How do we know that public resources are deployed efficiently and impactfully?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These are important questions, and I will explain why.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are thousands of courses and hundreds of training providers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are courses on Japanese finger painting and finger knitting.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There is a course listed titled "武侠小说系列探索", aimed at letting seniors relive their youth.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are courses on mindfulness, well-being and many on wine appreciation.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: One could argue that wine appreciation may be relevant for some professionals, but I was rather taken aback to learn that such classes are popular because participants can enjoy wine and snacks at lower costs than a wine bar, especially when fees are covered by SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There appears to be an attitude that since this is public money, one might as well spend it.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Some of these courses are eligible for both subsidies and credit usage.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: One example is a course on basic washroom cleaning, a useful life skill perhaps.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But I was surprised to discover that this course was offered by a provider that specialises in wine appreciation.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But as we move forward, some hard questions must be asked.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Do these courses truly align with the mission of the SkillsFuture movement and the broader mission of the new agency?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Is SkillsFuture the appropriate funding mechanism for them or would agencies like the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth or the People's Association be more suitable platforms?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Do such courses consume credits that could be deployed more impactfully elsewhere?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Do they dilute the mission and blur our understanding of how successful the scheme really is?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We should also ask how courses are curated.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Are they taking these courses to upgrade themselves meaningfully and are the training providers suitably qualified?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: My intention is not to criticise but to ask how we can do better.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I recognise the challenges of scaling and curating a large ecosystem, but this merger should bring renewed clarity and focus on higher objectives.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: To that end, I would like to make a suggestion.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: While some people have not used their SkillsFuture credits at all, others have deeply embraced lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Many of them are PMETs, a group significantly impacted by disruption.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They take specialised courses, stack micro credentials and pursue professional qualifications.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These pathways are more costly, but they are also more impactful.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: To me, those who are willing to put in more effort to better themselves deserves more support.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The most critical stakeholder here is the individual worker.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Everything that we are doing today – upskilling, AI initiatives, career services – prepares workers for the jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But we must also prepare them for the jobs of the day after tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The truth is, we simply do not know.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We foster not just lifelong learning but also resilience and adaptability.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The worker who thrives is not just one with the right skills but one with the right mindset, one who is agile, embraces change and is comfortable with uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our education system must equip our young, not just with knowledge but with the ability to adapt, pivot and confront the unknown.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: If we can align a well-calibrated system with a workforce that is resilient, agile and continuously learning, then we will be in a very strong position to meet the challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The former WDA, established in 2003, responded to structural shifts in our economy with a clear mandate – strengthen employability through a more systematic approach to skills development and CET.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It did so through initiatives, such as the WSQ framework, accreditation of training providers and funding for job-relevant courses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each agency addressed a different part of the employment cycle, with SSG adopting perhaps a "train first, and then find jobs" approach and WSG, a "find jobs, then train" model.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, if we assess how the system operates today, then several issues present themselves.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The "train first, then find jobs" approach runs the risk of creating incentives for training providers to prioritise course volume over employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some providers secure accreditation without clear evidence of labour market demand or meaningful links to career progression and then market these courses aggressively, sometimes targeting vulnerable groups, such as the elderly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes these courses are promoted with limited actual career pathways.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a result, SkillsFuture risked being seen less as a national upskilling effort and more as a commercial opportunity for some providers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The system is now crowded with courses of uneven quality, making it difficult for individuals to identify those that genuinely improve employability.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, the signalling value of SkillsFuture certifications has possibly weakened over time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employers cannot always distinguish between courses that build real capabilities and those that do not and therefore, do not consistently recognise these certifications with perhaps the same confidence as qualifications from our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This, again, weakens the link between training and hiring, and diminishes the value of the effort individuals invest in upskilling.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The "find jobs, then train" approach takes a different approach to the issue and faces a different constraint.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employers hire to meet immediate needs and prioritise candidates who can perform from the outset.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But for mid-career workers seeking to switch industries, this creates somewhat of a structural barrier.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They must demonstrate skills and experience they have not yet had the opportunity to acquire, making it a bit challenging and sometimes even difficult to access new roles not even when training support is available.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taken together, these approaches are not flawed in intent, but they are incomplete in isolation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One allows training to drift away from validated job demand and the other reflects demand but does not create sufficient entry points for those without prior experience.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By bringing together career guidance, skills development and job placement into a coherent system, we can better support Singaporeans across every stage of their working lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, funding largely follows enrolment and course completion, that is, a participation-based funding model.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But participation in courses alone is not the objective.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This anchors the system in real economic value.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Providers must demonstrate not only that individuals attend courses but that they benefit meaningfully in the labour market.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Providers will now be incentivised or will be motivated to design programmes aligned with validated market demand and deliver practical, job-relevant skills.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such courses will need to deliver these skills that can be translated into employable outcomes rather than just simply meeting accreditation requirements.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, it corrects misaligned incentives that have led to unintended outcomes, including the proliferation of low-value courses and those marketed aggressively to various vulnerable groups, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An outcome-based funding model reduces the viability of such offerings and re-focuses the ecosystem on meaningful skills development.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, and critically, it restores the credibility and employer recognition of SkillsFuture certifications.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By strengthening outcome-based discipline, we improve quality assurance, build employer trust and position SkillsFuture certificates as credible signals of capability, not just proof of course completion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This marks an important shift from participation to labour market signalling.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we must be clear, Sir, about the purpose of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is fundamentally an instrument of economic mobility and employability.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Its primary role is to help Singaporeans access better jobs, transition across sectors and progress in their careers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, this will not diminish the importance of personal enrichment.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Learning for interest, creativity or well-being remains valuable.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we should distinguish clearly between hobby-related learning or interest-related and job-linked training.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This preserves the spirit of lifelong learning while sharpening policy focus.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It directs public resources toward workforce outcomes without losing the broader benefits of learning for personal growth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have built substantial CET capacity across our IHLs, each offering a wide range of programmes through their respective CET centres.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this improves course access and diversity, we have yet to achieve coherence across the system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Courses from different IHLs could possibly overlap, compete or lack clear differentiation, leading to duplication and inefficiencies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SWDA can serve as a national planner, a coordinator, of CET supply and an aggregator of demand signals across sectors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It can coordinate sector-based course mapping to align programmes with industry needs and establish clearer differentiation across institutions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, ITE focusing on applied skills, polytechnics on industry practice and autonomous universities on advanced and specialised domains.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This allows institutions to complement rather than compete with one another.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, if SWDA is to deliver end-to-end support, we must look upstream.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, the system engages individuals largely after they enter the workforce or when they are actively seeking employment.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But misalignment often begins earlier, when students make decisions about subject combinations, courses of study and career pathways without possibly a clear understanding of what labour market realities are.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should, therefore, treat career guidance as a sort of early intervention policy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SWDA can work through strategic partnerships with IHL career centres and, where appropriate, with even MOE's education and career guidance ecosystem in secondary schools, junior colleges and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not about expanding SWDA's mandates, but about better aligning existing efforts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By connecting career guidance, training pathways and job opportunities, we can reduce downstream mismatches and give young Singaporeans greater clarity and confidence in navigating their careers at an early age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It represents a fundamental shift in how we think about work, skills and mobility in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not just about improving training systems.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is about how Singapore competes in an economy where industries reconfigure quickly, job roles evolve constantly and the shelf-life of skills continues to shorten.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our advantage can no longer rest on static qualifications.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It must rest on a system that enables continuous adaptation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this economy where jobs evolve faster than qualifications, our system must evolve faster than jobs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must give every Singaporean the confidence to move across roles, sectors and stages of life without being constrained by outdated skills or unclear pathways.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must strengthen not only employability, but also the dignity of work where the effort to upskill is recognised and where transitions are supported.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will signal continued commitment while reinforcing the importance of using these public resources meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, the success of SWDA will be measured by whether Singaporeans feel more confident navigating change whether they can learn, adapt and progress with assurance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is the system we must build: one that supports mobility, rewards effort and outcome, and gives every Singaporean the confidence to step forward, even as the ground beneath them continues to shift.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If one works hard and steadily, one is expected to move up.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But in today's economy, that is no longer the case.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A more accurate image may be a rock wall – one that is constantly changing and where there is no single fixed path upwards.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some routes are visible only to those who have been guided or trained to see them.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support this Bill because it strengthens three things: it clarifies our mission; it tightens our safeguards; it lays the foundation for a lifelong and person-centred view of work.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He took a SkillsFuture course in coffee-making and with a strong, enterprising spirit, he launched Hans Coffee, a hole-in-the wall cafe right in the heart of a wet market in Bishan!

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are the kinds of stories we want to see more of.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, not all SkillsFuture courses have had yielded such results.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite these setbacks, my resident continued to persevere, attending career fairs and employment programmes, and he demonstrated openness to take up different roles, even taking on a part-time assignment-based respite caregiver role.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He is waiting for confirmation on applications for programme executive roles, school administrative staff roles and even a role with the social service agency.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a far cry from the IT role he had trained and applied for.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He wrote, "I remain committed to securing full-time employment and contributing meaningful to the workforce.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sharing my situation as I feel that while training support is available, there appear to be gaps in translating training into actual employment opportunities, availability of suitable entry-roles for mid-career individuals, post-event follow-up and job matching support.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, it would be very helpful if there could be structured, on-the-job training, practical attachments or industry-based training opportunities to allow individuals, like myself, to gain relevant hands-on experience." I hope SWDA will consider my resident's requests and I also hope that SWDA, as a single agency, with responsibility for identifying current and emerging skills in close partnership with industries and tripartite partners, can help provide jobseekers with better clarity and concrete pathways that show which courses to take, which work-study options to consider and which jobs are realistically within reach.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, this Bill strengthens safeguards and raises standards.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we encourage people to invest their time and savings into training, we carry a responsibility to keep them safe from bad actors.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have seen how some providers try to exploit subsidies or use misleading marketing to pull learners in.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I, therefore, welcome the stronger tools enacted in this Bill to act against abusive funding arrangements and false advertising.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, this Bill opens the way to a more lifelong and human-centred approach to work.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is often an outpouring of a person's purpose and sense of identity.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When someone is displaced from work, the impact ripples through the household.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Children worry about money, caregivers feel guilt and stress, and the family's collective mental health can suffer.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The integrated mandate of this agency gives us a chance to design support that sees the core and the heart of the whole person, and not just the vacancy to be filled.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am encouraged that the agency will work with schools, IHLs, employers and tripartite partners.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope it will also work closely with community partners and social service agencies.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of those who struggle most with training and transitions face multiple stressors at the same time, including caregiving responsibilities, chronic illness, housing challenges and debt.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When these issues remain unaddressed, even the best-designed course or job match may not last.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With all of these, Mr Speaker, I have several questions for the Government as we look ahead to execution and the longer term.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will the Government ensure that the transition from SSG and WSG to the new agency is seamless from the public's perspective?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, on long-term plans in a changing economy.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We know that the pace of change will accelerate as AI, demographic shifts and climate transition reshape entire sectors.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will it move beyond reactive job-matching to help firms proactively redesign career trajectories, ensuring the wider labour force will be meaningfully uplifted, rather than being left to face these shifts alone?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How might the agency evolve to support increasingly salient forms of work, such as gig workers, freelancers and those in informal care roles who may not fit neatly into traditional employer-employee models?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And will the agency track and report not just training participation, but also outcomes, like wage progression, job stability and well-being, so that Singaporeans can see whether the system is truly working for all of them together?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, on supporting those at greatest risk of being left behind.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this House, I have spoken before about what it feels like to be at the margins and to feel that the system is not set up for you.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many lower-income workers, older workers and caregivers express similar anxieties.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They know that there are many schemes, yet they do not know where to start and they worry that they cannot keep up.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we, as a nation, leave people to fend for themselves in a race that only some can win, or do we commit to walking with them as they learn, work and care?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe this new agency is key to a further and necessary shift in our national psyche.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the last decade, SkillsFuture has successfully changed the mindset of our society toward the necessity of lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To return to the analogy of the rock wall that I used at the beginning of my speech, the SWDA is the rope system, anchored firmly by the state, employers and unions together.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It ensures that when a worker reaches for a hold and slips, they are not left to fall without support, but are given the safety to regain their footing, to be guided back to the wall and to continue their ascent with renewed confidence and clearer direction.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope that as we build this new agency, we hold fast to a simple measure of success: that more Singaporeans, especially those who feel anxious today, can say with confidence that even if they stumble in their climb, they are not alone and they are able to rise again.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some are fresh jobseekers, anxious about their first step into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many are older workers and mid-career PMEs, trying to find their footing again after displacement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One resident, Mr K, came to see me.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He met a job coach, worked on his curriculum vitae, took advice, followed through on what was recommended.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But he still could not land a job.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When he came back again, it was not because he had not tried.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It was because, in his own words, the problem was not effort but his age.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And it was the gap between what he had hoped for and what the market was willing to offer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am sure many Members have similar stories to tell.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As this is an enabling Bill, Parliament's responsibility is not only to examine the powers that are being created, but to ask a deeper question.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What outcomes will these powers guarantee for our people?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My residents, especially older workers, displaced PMEs and fresh graduates do not merely need a larger agency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They need earlier help, clearer pathways, fairer decisions and measurable results.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is in this spirit that I seek clarifications in five areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, on the strategic rationale of the merger.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We began with one agency more than a decade ago under the WDA, moved to two with SSG and WSG and now returning to one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, the fundamental question is not whether integration sounds right.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What could not be done under two agencies that now requires a single statutory board with a consolidated and expanded mandate under section 5?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the problem is fragmentation between agencies, then consolidation is logical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But if the problem lies in execution on the ground, then merging agencies alone may not solve anything.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 5 confers a broad mandate, including additional functions assigned by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, clause 6 gives the agency wide-ranging operational powers, from funding to partnerships.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This reinforces the need for clarity on how such broad discretion will translate into better outcomes for residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are we streamlining the system or are we concentrating complexity within a single institution?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The real test is whether this design will improve outcomes for residents like Mr K.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For displaced PMEs and older workers, timing determines outcome.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Support that comes from redundancy often comes too late.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill gives the agency the power to act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it does not impose a duty to act early.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 5(1)(g) allows the collection and analysis of labour market data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But such data has already been collected across agencies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The question is not data collection, but whether data now leads to earlier and more decisive intervention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will it be wage decline, sector disruption or repeated job transitions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will outreach be proactive or still largely reactive?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if decisions are data driven, what resources does a resident have, if the system misclassifies risk?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When we speak of success, how will it be measured?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To strengthen this pillar, I suggest: first, clear triggers for proactive intervention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, public reporting on time to placement and retention outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And third, defined governance and appeal mechanisms for data and AI-driven decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because for residents like Mr K, help that comes too late does not change the outcome.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is about how residents experience the system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill defines functions and powers, but it does not define service guarantees.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But coordination must translate into a real experience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will residents be case managed end-to-end, or will they still move across multiple touchpoints?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will MyCareersFuture and MySkillsFuture be streamlined under SWDA to provide a truly integrated, one-stop platform for individuals?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If these platforms remain separate, we risk preserving fragmentation in the user journey, even as we merge agencies at the top.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the intention is seamless service, why is there no explicit "no wrong door" commitment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This matters especially for older workers and residents who require high-touch support.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If these codes are non-legislative, how will Parliament know what standards are actually being enforced in practice?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To make the system real for residents, I suggest that we need: first, a formal "no wrong door" protocol.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, published service standards for response and case continuity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And third, transparency on digital versus assisted access.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because residents, like Mr K, do not see agencies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They experience whether someone stays with them throughout the journey or whether they are passed along.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, on quality and funding.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is about what we fund and what we measure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the system did not deliver the outcome he needed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Courses that are technically compliant but may not improve employability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What mechanisms will SWDA put in place to ensure that training curricula of its funded courses are tightly aligned with industry demand and not lagging behind it?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be stronger accountability for training providers whose programmes do not lead to actual job placements?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also avoid a system where providers focus only on easy cases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Those who need the most support must not be left behind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because for residents, like Mr K, training is not the goal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That ensures continuity at the point of merger.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Once integration begins in earnest, what is the plan for restructuring?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must provide clarity to those who will implement this system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also clarify the role of ecosystem partners, especially NTUC and e2i.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the Bill does not define their role in the new structure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because integration at the top must not lead to fragmentation below.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But effort did not lead to a desirable outcome.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is the gap this Bill must close.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because we are not just preparing Singaporeans for the jobs of today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are also preparing them for the jobs of tomorrow in a future shaped by technology and AI.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Prime Minister reminded us in Budget 2026 and also at May Day that AI will transform the way we work, the way businesses operate and the way jobs are created.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Skills will age more quickly, industries will shift faster and workers will have to adapt continuously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, the question before us is not just how we help someone find a job.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The question is whether we are building a system that helps Singaporeans stay employable and employed over a lifetime.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Vice Chair of the Health GPC, I often reflect on how we approach healthcare.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We do not wait for people to fall sick before we act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We screen early, we intervene upstream and we support individuals over time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should take the same approach to careers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It should help Singaporeans monitor their career health, anticipate change and act early.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if I may summarise the key points I have raised in my speech.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, all of these come down to one test.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When a person steps forward, when he invests his time in training, when he does everything right, does that training lead to a job and does that job last?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because without that, the system risks measuring effort, not outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If SWDA can track that, measure it and act on it, then residents, like Mr K, will not have to come back again asking for help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And this system will not just deliver programmes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In that regard, I therefore support the Bill to merge and form the SWDA, but I have some clarifications on some of the underlying principles, perceptions and operational issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is an obvious synergy between the educational and training work that is currently spearheaded by SSG, and the workforce design and transformation that is supported by WSG.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After all, both agencies were restructured out of the WDA that was set up in 2003 to focus on CET to mitigate against job displacement of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be helpful for Singaporeans to understand that this is not merely a bureaucratic combination, but a transformational change where one plus one gives you more than two.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Post-merger, how would existing initiatives and programmes be continued and/or enhanced?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially with the skills and jobs initiatives and workgroups that have only been rolled out in the past 12 months or so, such as AfA-ACES and the Tripartite Workgroup on Human Capital Capability Development (TWG-HC).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More fundamentally, this brings up the question of how we have been measuring the success of our skills and jobs transformation efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There may be some perception that the merger is unnecessary wastage since we had split the WDA to create SSG and WSG in 2016, and now we are bridging it under one umbrella agency again.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From my reading of the Hansard, I do not think there is any inconsistency between the rationale behind creating SSG to create better synergies with MOE and education institutions, and the SWDA's objective of a unified strategy for the training, career and employment services ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But perhaps the Minister could help to assuage any such concerns.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I expect that some costs will need to be expended for rebranding, including on materials and collaterals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, has there been any assessment of the costs of the increased size of the organisation, along with any associated externalities?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding the vesting provisions at clause 68 of the Bill, I presume there will also be administrative costs in reflecting changes to the bank accounts, property and funds held by the respective agencies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond organisational structure, the effectiveness of the SWDA will ultimately depend on how quickly it can translate industry signals into skills development and training outcomes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the role of these members and what kind of knowledge, skills and experience would these members be expected to possess?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would this be a tripartite group in and of itself, or is it expected that the new SWDA will continually engage with and partner NTUC and the Singapore National Employers' Federation (SNEF) in devising and executing its plans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is the relationship between the new SWDA, NTUC and SNEF expected to be like on a working level?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Minister also elaborate on the intended composition of the SWDA Board and the types of knowledge, skills and experience that these members are expected to bring?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the fast-changing nature of the global economy and labour market, it would be useful to understand whether there will be strong representation from the private sector, particularly senior HR practitioners and business leaders at the managing director level and above from multinational corporations and leading local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such practitioners are often at the frontline of hiring, skills transformation and workforce planning, and are therefore well-placed to provide timely insights into emerging skills gaps and evolving job roles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Their perspectives could help ensure that SWDA remains closely attuned to real-world industry developments and is able to respond more quickly to shifts in demand.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, will there be mechanisms beyond Board representation, such as advisory panels or sector-specific councils, to systematically capture and incorporate these industry insights into policy design and programme implementation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For public servants that are currently serving under SSG and WSG, may I ask how would their roles be restructured or reorganised after the merger?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While clauses 69 and 70 of the Bill seek to transfer every SSG and WSG employee to the new SWDA and present their employment terms, I do not suppose the intention is for every such employee to retain their current portfolios in the new and enhanced SWDA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Prime Minister's Budget 2026 speech also announced that the new SWDA will be jointly overseen by the MOM and the MOE, some of the Members before me have already mentioned this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When the proposed WSDA Bill refers to "Minister" without specifying his/her portfolio, for example at clauses 1, 4 and 7, does that refer to the Minister for Manpower or the Minister for Education?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It may be helpful to have a simple, graphical representation of the allocation of Ministerial responsibility, so that it is clear to members of the public, or even us Members of Parliament, on who we should be raising specific SWDA-related issues to.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While our institutions have done well to update programmes periodically, there may be scope to move towards a more dynamic and iterative model of curriculum design.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would help, importantly, ensure that our students graduate not just with qualifications, but with skills that are immediately relevant and adaptable to the needs of employers and are not redundant in five years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Amidst rapid technological advancements, such as AI and geopolitical shifts that are getting more uncertain and unpredictable, change is the only constant.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must continue to keep our world-leading and maturing workforce nimble, so that we can capitalise on the opportunities that spring up and capture value and good jobs for Singaporeans today and tomorrow and for our students still in school, in our IHLs, at the moment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: SSG focused on kickstarting and building lifelong learning and continuing education among Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: WSG focused on job matching and employment support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Both agencies have made real contributions over the past decade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The question before us today is whether our institutions are still suited to the labour market that Singaporeans now face.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This Bill is a timely and necessary response to a changed world of work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In the past, we could treat skills and employment as two separate journeys.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: You went to school to get skills and then you went to the job market to find work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: But today, skills and work are tied together in an ongoing journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It does not mean workers expect the Government to guarantee every job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Singaporeans understand that change and disruption are part of modern working life, but they do expect something fair and fundamental.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: If you work hard, learnt and adapt, they should have a fair chance to progress, to move into new opportunities and to provide for their families with dignity and confidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Career security is not the promise of no disruption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is a promise that workers will not be left alone to navigate disruption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Back in 2016, I argued that training and job outcomes must stay connected.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The true test of a policy is not how many people attend the course or how many certificates are handed out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The real test is whether workers can move into better jobs and feel more confident about the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Right now, the system can feel a bit fragmented for some workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They might get career guidance in one office.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They go to another place for training advice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: When you are in the middle of a stressful career change, this fragmented journey can make things appear harder.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: You are left to bridge the gaps yourself.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It will link business transformation, training and employment support into a smoother workstream.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We must remember that training, by itself, is not enough if the jobs themselves are not being redesigned.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Skills training must match work, how work is actually being organised in the real world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: When merging these agencies, we ensure that training is always tied to real industry needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Many workers are not only worried about losing their jobs, they are worried about falling behind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They are worried that the skills they have today may not be enough for tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: When workers make the effort to upskill but cannot see how that leads to better jobs or real mobility, confidence in the system starts to weaken.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: And when effort no longer appears to lead to opportunity, the issue is not just economic, it is social as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: One area that deserves close attention is what some have called the broken rung, something I spoke about during my Budget speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Many academics and researchers have also spoken up on this matter, and you will find increasing literature on this topic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: For young people, the first foothold in the labour market matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It shapes confidence, habits, skills and future earnings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It often sets the direction of an entire career, but today the first rung is less secure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: New technologies, including AI, are changing what firms expect, even from those just entering the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: For some young workers, the challenge is no longer simply finding a job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: If the first rung weakens, it affects progression, wage growth and long-term mobility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The old assumption that one can simply enter, learn on a job and move up steadily can no longer be taken for granted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They need better information on where demand is growing and training that is more closely tied to real workplace needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They may also need more support in moving from school to work and from first job to a sustainable career.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This is where a more integrated agency can make a real difference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: When the same system can connect career guidance, training advice, market labour signals and employment support, it becomes easier to help younger Singaporeans where they are most likely to fall through the cracks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This effort requires the full strength of tripartism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Government can shape policy and provide systems of support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Employers create jobs, redesign work and invest in their people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Unions bring workers' voice, trust and a deep understanding of how change is felt on the ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Training providers helped turn broad ambition to practical capability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We recently announced the Tripartite Jobs Council on May Day.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This Council will help workers and the businesses navigate the big changes brought by AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It will work hand-in-hand with the SWDA to make sure that businesses adopt new technology, that workers are trained and supported to move into new roles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to support this effort in concrete ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: NTUC has a long-standing partnership with Government on business transformation, training and worker support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Through our unions and our work on the ground, we see where anxieties are rising and where support is most needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We can help workers and employers understand where opportunities lie and navigate the path from uncertainty to action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The e2i will continue its deep partnership with the new agency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Over the years, WSG has transferred various career jobs and skills centres to e2i, enabling it to serve more jobseekers on the ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Building on this foundation, e2i can work closely with the new agency to translate national strategies into practical support through direct engagement with workers and businesses on career guidance, job matching and workforce transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: As the broken rung becomes a more real concern, support should begin earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Career guidance should not only start after a young person struggles to find work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It should begin before graduation and continue through the early career years, where expectations are shifting quickly and confidence is still being formed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: First, e2i can and will bring its labour market knowledge, employer network and ground-sensing to partnerships with IHLs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: For many mid-career workers, the fear is not only just change itself but the cost of change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: A transition may mean temporary income loss, uncertainty for the family and real doubt about whether a new path will work out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Workers need support – the lower the friction of transition, it gives them greater confidence to make a move when change becomes necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: With the merger of this agency, we should consider a few things.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This is where a worker is matched to a job before they start training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It gives them certainty of a pay cheque and a clear path forward, reducing the stress in their lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: NTUC Learning Hub can further support this new social compact by helping workers and employers translate transformation into capability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We know training only works if it is tied to a real job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Through our Company Training Committees, we help companies, especially small businesses, figure out how to redesign their work and help their workers to improve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: NTUC Learning Hub can play a vital role here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They build skills pathways that industries actually value.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: For example, the Tech Talent Academy works with tech firms like AWS, Microsoft and Goggle to train and place workers into tech jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: More than half of them have already found jobs in a softening job market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This shows that when we link training directly to employment, better things can happen.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: If this new agency can help Singapore move closer to that goal, it will build the social compact for a new era of work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The Government has an important role, but it cannot do this alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: NTUC will continue with the new SWDA to strength career security for workers at every stage of their life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This Bill is an important step towards building that compact for workers for today and tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will attempt to address all of them holistically.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will group the issues raised thematically and of course, reply to the questions as best as possible.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have decided to group it into eight broad pillars.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, raising the quality as well as the forms of training.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Three, connecting training to matching them to good jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Five, become even more proactive and to provide anticipatory support.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Six, what are the outcome measures of success.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Seven, the governance of the new merged entity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And of course, eight, last but not least, on transition and continuity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, I would like to address some fundamental questions raised over the purpose of this merger.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In particular, Mr Gerald Giam characterised the merger as a reversal of the position from 2016.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is more important to ask if the restructuring in 2016 was the right call then and whether the merger, moving forward is the right call now and for the future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The restructuring in 2016 allowed SSG and WSG to develop specialised capabilities in adult training and employment facilitation respectively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The House then supported the Skills Future Singapore Agency Bill in 2016.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Giam's former colleague, Mr Leon Pereira, supported the aim to bring about a far-reaching change in our adult education and training landscape by establishing an agency that is solely focused on adult education in ways that are intimately linked to economic goals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Through SSG's nexus with MOE, the IHLs have become the key pillars of CET delivery today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Meanwhile, WSG expanded public employment services and introduced new programmes to address mismatches.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Both agencies have substantially achieved the objectives of the restructuring.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Earlier on, when I gave the speech, I elaborated extensively on the achievements of SSG and WSG.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The next bound of our workforce strategy requires an end-to-end system that connects skills to jobs more quickly and more accurately than before.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It requires a more integrated structure so that we can be more agile and nimble in predicting, in pre-empting and preparing for new opportunities and disruptions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is what will make SWDA more than the sum of its parts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To address Mr Saktiandi Supaat's question, this is a key function in the SWDA Bill which goes beyond those in the SSG and the WSG Act.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we must not lose the specialised capabilities that we have built over the past 10 years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Shawn Loh rightly highlighted the importance of preserving the strong relationship between IHLs and the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And Assoc Prof Terence Ho asked how we will ensure that IHLs will continue to develop as institutions of lifelong learning.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Through MOE's joint oversight of SWDA, we will continue to deepen this relationship, strengthen complementarity between IHLs and private training providers and improve coordination between CET and pre-employment training.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, this is not a two-headed monster.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is a two-horse chariot, pulling in the same direction, charging ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi and Mr Giam asked about the costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Similarly, the merger also not require additional budget allocation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will be some costs incurred for branding, marketing and systems integration.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These costs would have been budgeted for any regular refreshes, even if there was no merger.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These costs will be managed within the existing budgets of SSG and WSG, and their reserves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the second point, raising the quality and the focus of training, Ms Gho Sze Kee asked about the curation of SkillsFuture courses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: She is right that not everything in the SkillsFuture catalogue has been directed towards our workforce development goals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But SkillsFuture is much more than just training for industry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SkillsFuture is a national movement to promote a culture of lifelong learning.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Remember I kept emphasising earlier on about getting everyone to have that mindset change.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, how do we initiate them, how do we start them into that habit, that matters.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In response to Assoc Prof Terence Ho's question, lifelong learning that is not targeted at employment will still come under SWDA's purview.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SWDA will work with agencies, such as the People's Association on the curation of such programmes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we encourage all Singaporeans to learn not just for their current job, or the next job, but also in their areas of interest.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Not all training leads to immediate employment and wage gains.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On a third group, connecting and matching training to good jobs, it is essential that SWDA's good work is closely linked to industry and of top tier quality.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, unlike what Mr Tiong shared earlier on, there are significant guardrails to ensuring that SkillsFuture courses are top quality, with industry playing a big role in ensuring the relevance of training.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our trade associations and chambers, and professional bodies, they come together to help curate and signpost courses and some employers serve as SkillsFuture Queen Bees to provide training for other companies, including SMEs in their respective sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As SWDA, we will work with industry to play an even bigger role, which also brings me to my second point.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think Mr Tiong, perhaps, may not have fully understood.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is not just an individual credit scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SkillsFuture sits alongside the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit, which employers can use to send their workers for training.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These employers and individuals need to co-pay for training programmes, whether through their credits or out-of-pocket, and they must also invest their time and effort.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Companies and workers must choose the best courses worth their while and training providers must regularly up the game to compete.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government, of course, plays a role in regulating the provider, the course and adult educator as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And as pointed out by Ms Jessica Tan, our success depends on the ecosystem: on the individuals, employers and other stakeholders and partners playing a big role.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This ecosystem is, therefore, central to the SkillsFuture movement and will continue to be so under SWDA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Mr Darryl David rightly pointed out, SkillsFuture is fundamentally an instrument of economic mobility and employability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This now brings me to the core of SWDA's mandate and that is to support Singaporeans at every stage of their careers through promoting lifelong learning, strengthening their career health and enhancing access to good jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Dr Wan Rizal identified two distinct gaps that SWDA must close.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The first-job gap for fresh graduates and the career transition gap for mid-careerists.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Darryl David highlighted that students often make decisions about courses and career pathways without a clear understanding of labour market realities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Desmond Choo and Ms Jessica Tan also raised concerns on how SWDA will support entry-level hiring amidst business restructuring and AI-driven change.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On supporting fresh graduates to get their first jobs, I agree with Dr Wan Rizal and Mr Darryl David that we cannot wait until students graduate before we intervene.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SWDA will work with IHLs and MOE to bring industry exposure upstream so that our students can have a clearer picture of the labour market well before they graduate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am not confident that we can go all the way to the secondary school as suggested by a Member here, but we certainly will go upstream to bring the industry exposure to our undergraduates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This means more systematic pathways into industry attachments and clearer signals on skills and roles in demand.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we will review measures to better support graduates who face difficulties in securing employment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To support mid-careerists to chart their careers amidst a fast-evolving world, SWDA will empower them to take charge and strengthen their career health.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The calls from Mr Darryl David, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Shawn Loh and Assoc Prof Terence Ho to tighten the nexus between training grants and employment outcomes are directionally aligned with our plans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Dr Neo Kok Beng's suggestion for SWDA to partner professional institutions to align training to professional accreditations will also help to ensure that the skills acquired are recognised by the industry and can pave the way for career progression.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also supporting Singaporeans to acquire the skills and the perspectives needed for a globalised economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The OMIP that Mr Tiong talked about allows companies to send to Singaporeans on overseas postings to build first-hand knowledge of international markets and bring these insights back home.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We agree that such schemes can be made accessible to benefit even more Singaporeans and we had announced at the Committee of Supply this year that we will be expanding OMIP to young professionals even earlier in their careers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Supporting our workers to acquire skills, experience and career agility is only part of the equation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To maximise their potential, workers must also be able to signal their skills and experience to employers, be matched to jobs that make use of these skills and experience and to be rewarded fairly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To this end, SWDA will also work to reduce information asymmetries in the labour market to facilitate more efficient job matching.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MyCareersFuture.gov.sg will continue to be our national jobs bank, where good jobs are visible, accessible and intelligently matched to jobseekers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To strengthen the pipeline of quality job listings, MOM, SWDA and sector agencies will work together to encourage more companies to list vacancies on the portal.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have forged partnerships with five online job portals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singaporeans can use verified employment history and training data in their Careers and Skills Passport to apply for jobs on these job portals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In line with SWDA's expanded mandate, we will build ecosystem enablers, such as data sharing mechanisms and accreditation frameworks, to facilitate faster and better job matches.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The fourth pillar: catering to diverse and ever-changing needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Several Members have asked how SWDA will serve the diverse needs of workers and employers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Dr Hamid Razak, Ms Elysa Chen, Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Melvin Yong, Ms He Ting Ru and Ms Jessica Tan have asked about worker segments, such as caregivers, seniors, persons with disabilities, ex-offenders and those who have experienced health setbacks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will partner community organisations, like SG Enable, Yellow Ribbon Singapore and Community Development Councils, to reach the more vulnerable segments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Mr Melvin Yong suggested, we are also studying ways to provide stronger support for more flexible work models, such as fractional work, that may better cater to their needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: NTUC is spearheading the Company Training Committee initiative, which involves $300 million funding to drive enterprise and workforce transformation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Echoing Mr Desmond Choo, the Labour Movement will continue to be a strategic partner of SWDA in translating national strategies to practical support by providing high-touch support to different worker segments through employment facilitation, training and workforce transformation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For employers, they also have diverse needs depending on their industry size, sector and business development plans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Mark Lee asked whether support will be differentiated for SMEs and large enterprises and whether SWDA will retain sector-specific expertise.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SWDA will tailor its strategies to better suit the different profiles of the companies that it serves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In line with suggestions from Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Ms Eileen Chong, Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Shawn Loh, Mr Mark Lee and Assoc Prof Terence Ho, SWDA will also explore ways to step up support for job redesign and on-job-training so that training is customised to different workplaces and different business models, helping our workers to take on higher-value-added jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling called for SWDA to support more companies in job redesign and workforce transformation, just like FairPrice Store of Tomorrow at Punggol.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will indeed be a priority for SWDA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
